materials.title: The Quiet Cost of a Campus App: Reading Trends, Comparisons and Proportions
materials.instructions: 本材料为项目原创模拟场景、人物与数据，不是官方雅思试题，也未经考生难度标定。阅读全文后完成10题；区分原始说法、证据、推断与不确定事项。所有题干与选项为英文，解析为中文。填空按题目词数和原文词形作答。语法先学习规则，再完成8项独立新句或新数据练习。口语与写作迁移另用自己的新细节；完成本练习不等于独立能力已达标。
materials.passage:
A. In September, a small university in the north of England began a twelve-week trial of a new campus app called CampusFlow. The app was designed to help students find empty study rooms, check library opening hours, and receive alerts about timetable changes. The project team, led by Dr. Helen Marsh, expected the app to reduce the time students spent searching for information. They also hoped it would lower the number of missed classes caused by last-minute room changes. The trial involved 1,200 students across three faculties: Science, Arts, and Business. At the start, 62% of participants said they used paper timetables or noticeboards as their main source of information. Only 18% used the university's existing website, and 20% relied on messages from friends. These baseline figures provided a clear picture of how students accessed information before the app was introduced, and they gave the team a reliable point of comparison for measuring later change.

B. By the end of the trial, the picture had changed considerably. The proportion of students using the app as their main source of information rose from 0% to 54%. Use of paper timetables and noticeboards fell sharply, from 62% to 21%. The website's share dropped slightly, from 18% to 15%, while reliance on friends' messages declined from 20% to 10%. Dr. Marsh noted that the app was most popular among first-year students: 71% of them used it daily, compared with 43% of second-year students and only 29% of final-year students. She suggested that final-year students had already developed reliable personal networks and therefore felt less need for a central tool. This pattern suggests that the app's value may be highest for those who are new to the university environment, since they have fewer established habits and contacts to rely on.

C. The team also measured missed classes. In the twelve weeks before the trial, the three faculties recorded an average of 84 missed classes per week due to room changes. During the trial, this figure fell to 57 per week. However, the improvement was not equal across faculties. Science saw the largest drop, from 31 to 14 missed classes per week. Arts fell from 28 to 22, and Business from 25 to 21. Dr. Marsh warned that these numbers should be treated with caution. "The autumn term is always quieter than the spring term," she said. "We cannot assume that the app alone caused the fall." Other factors, such as the time of year and the specific courses running, could also have influenced attendance. For example, the autumn term may include fewer field trips or practical sessions that are easily disrupted by room changes, so part of the improvement may reflect the normal seasonal pattern rather than the app itself.

D. Student feedback revealed hidden assumptions in the project's original design. The team had assumed that all students owned smartphones with reliable internet access. In fact, 9% of participants reported that their phones often lost connection in older buildings. The team had also assumed that students would check the app before every class. Interviews showed that many students checked it only once a day, usually in the morning. One Business student explained, "I look at it with breakfast. After that, I'm too busy." Another assumption was that clearer information would automatically lead to better attendance. Yet several Arts students said they missed classes because of part-time jobs, not because they were confused about rooms. These findings highlight the gap between designers' expectations and students' actual daily routines, and they show why testing a tool with real users matters.

E. The app's usage statistics showed a clear weekly pattern. Activity was highest on Mondays, when 68% of users opened the app at least once. It declined steadily through the week, reaching 41% on Fridays. Weekend use was very low, at 12% on Saturdays and 9% on Sundays. The team found this trend unsurprising, since most classes take place on weekdays. However, they were surprised by the age difference: students aged 18 to 20 used the app almost twice as often as students aged 25 and over. The older group reported that they preferred email reminders, which they could read on larger screens. This preference suggests that communication channels may need to be tailored to different age groups rather than relying on a single app for everyone.

F. The final report recommended three changes. First, the app should work offline, storing the latest timetable on the phone. Second, the team should send a single daily email summary to students who prefer email. Third, the university should collect better data on why students miss classes, separating room confusion from other reasons such as work or illness. Dr. Marsh concluded, "A useful tool is not the same as a complete solution. We need to compare what we hoped would happen with what actually happened." The university will decide in January whether to continue the app for all 8,000 students, and the trial results will form the main evidence for that decision.

grammar.title: 数据句的时态、比较、百分比与百分点
grammar.explanation: 复习：明确结束的过去时间用一般过去时；from说明起点，to说明终点，by说明变化量。本课新增：比例从8%到12%增加4个百分点，却是相对原比例增加50%，percent与percentage points不能互换。比较比例须保持分母和指标可比，不能因人数相同就说比例相同。twice that at...可避免把比例同地点直接比较。the proportion/percentage作主语通常按单数处理。描述变化延续至今可用现在完成时。compared with和compared to在很多比较语境均可用，than后省略重复动词也可能正确；不把合法变体当错项。先后变化不自动证明因果，要保留证据限制。以下均为新模拟数据句。

materials.instructions: 本材料为项目原创模拟场景、人物与数据，不是官方雅思试题，也未经考生难度标定。先听分角色美式合成录音，再答10题；留意说话人的更正、条件和立场。录音未重做前不可把旧音频配给本稿。所有题干与选项为英文，解析为中文。填空按题目词数和原文词形作答。语法先学习规则，再完成8项独立新句或新数据练习。口语与写作迁移另用自己的新细节；完成本练习不等于独立能力已达标。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Hi, everyone. Thanks for coming to the student technology committee meeting. I'm Maya, and I run the committee this term. We're here to talk about the new campus shuttle app. The pilot starts next Monday, and we need to decide what to recommend to the university. Let's start with the data from last month's survey. Ben, can you give us the numbers?

Ben: Sure. We asked 400 students about the old shuttle system. Only 28 percent said they were satisfied with the current app. That's a big problem. But when we asked about the new app, 65 percent said they would probably use it. That's a huge jump.

Maya: Wait, Ben, let me check that. You said 65 percent would probably use it? I thought the number was 56 percent.

Ben: Oh, you're right. Sorry, I mixed up two surveys. The 65 percent was for the library app. For the shuttle app, it's 56 percent. So, 56 percent said they would probably use the new shuttle app.

Maya: Thanks for correcting that. Fifty-six is twice twenty-eight, but that doesn't mean satisfaction has doubled. One answer reports current satisfaction; the other predicts possible use. We must keep those measures separate. What about the cost?

Ben: The new app costs $12,000 to develop. The old app costs $8,000 a year to maintain. The new app will cost $5,000 a year to maintain. So, in the first year, the total cost is $17,000. After that, it's $5,000 a year. The old app is $8,000 every year. So, the new app saves money after about two years.

Maya: Hold on. The yearly maintenance saving is only three thousand dollars. It takes four years to recover the twelve-thousand-dollar development cost. At the end of year four, each option totals thirty-two thousand, assuming these costs stay unchanged.

Ben: You're right. Lower annual maintenance is not the same as a lower total cost immediately. From year five, the new app would be cheaper overall, unless extra costs arose.

Maya: Now, let's talk about the hidden assumptions. Some students assume the new app will work everywhere on campus. But the pilot only covers the main campus. The north campus is not included yet. That's an important limitation.

Ben: Right. Also, some people think the app will show real-time bus locations. But in the pilot, it only shows scheduled times. Real-time tracking comes later, maybe next year.

Maya: So, we need to be careful about what we promise. The survey shows interest, but the pilot is limited. Let's recommend the pilot, but with clear information about these limits. Any questions?

Ben: One more thing. The survey also asked about the old app's problems. The top problem was that it often crashed. 45 percent of students said it crashed at least once a week. The new app is designed to crash less, but we don't have data yet.

Maya: During the pilot, let's record failures per one hundred attempted checks, not just total complaints. If twice as many people try the app, the number of complaints could rise even when the failure rate falls.

Ben: And we should compare the same routes and times of day. Otherwise a quieter service could make the app seem more reliable. We can report the limits alongside the results.

Maya: Okay. So, our recommendation: support the pilot, but tell students about the limited coverage and the scheduled times only. And we should collect data during the pilot. Does everyone agree?

Ben: Yes, I agree.

Maya: Great. Let's meet again in two weeks to review the first pilot data. Thanks, everyone.

questions.prompt: A share moved from 25% to 40%. Which statement is accurate?
questions.explanation: 40%-25%=15个百分点；相对增长15/25=60%，两种单位不能互换。
questions.evidence: The share increased by 15 percentage points, from 25% to 40%.

questions.prompt: Choose the past-tense form: The number of complaints ______ from 80 to 60 during last year's trial.
questions.explanation: last year指定结束的过去时间；fall的过去式是fell，不是fall的被动形式。
questions.evidence: The number of complaints fell from 80 to 60 during last year's trial.

questions.prompt: Of 200 respondents, 50 supported a proposal. Which proportion is correct?
questions.evidence: Twenty-five percent of the respondents supported the proposal.

questions.prompt: Twenty of 50 cyclists and twenty of 100 drivers reported delays. Which comparison is accurate?
options: The shares were equal because the counts were equal.
The share among cyclists was 20 percent.
The share among drivers was twice the share among cyclists.
The share among cyclists was twice the share among drivers.
answers: The share among cyclists was twice the share among drivers.
questions.explanation: 骑车者20/50=40%，驾车者20/100=20%；相同人数不代表相同比例。
questions.evidence: The share among cyclists was twice the share among drivers.

questions.prompt: Complete the present-tense statement: Thirty percent of the equipment ______ unavailable.
questions.explanation: 这里实际对象是不可数单数equipment，现在时用is。percent of后不能不看名词就一律用复数动词。
questions.evidence: Thirty percent of the equipment is unavailable.

questions.prompt: Keep the comparison parallel: The average journey in Town A was longer than ______.
questions.explanation: that替代单数the average journey；不能把旅程与城市或人直接比较，those是复数替代。
questions.evidence: The average journey in Town A was longer than that in Town B.

questions.prompt: A survey records plans to buy a ticket, not actual purchases. Which report stays within that evidence?
options: The survey confirms that all future customers are satisfied.
The survey suggests possible demand but does not establish actual sales.
The number of plans is identical to the number of completed sales.
The survey proves that every planned purchase has already occurred.
answers: The survey suggests possible demand but does not establish actual sales.
questions.explanation: 意向能提示潜在需求，不能当成已完成购买或满意度证据。The survey suggests possible demand but does not establish actual sales 保留了这一证据边界。
questions.evidence: The survey suggests possible demand but does not establish actual sales.

questions.prompt: Revision: choose the future passive form. The next survey ______ in November.
questions.explanation: survey是被开展的对象；未来被动为will be conducted。
questions.evidence: The next survey will be conducted in November.

materials.title: When Algorithms Decide: A Panel on Limits
materials.instructions: 阅读一篇关于算法决策边界的模拟教育材料（非官方雅思测试）。先通读文章，理解大意；再完成10道题（单选、填空、判断正误/未提及）。注意数据句的准确性、趋势与比较表达。语法部分先看中文讲解，再完成8道新句子的语法题。最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。所有答案必须依据原文。
materials.passage:
A city council in the fictional town of Riverton formed a panel to examine how algorithms are used in public services. The panel, called the Algorithm Review Group (ARG), met for the first time in March. Its task was to consider the limits of algorithmic decisions in three areas: school admissions, traffic fines, and social housing. The group included teachers, parents, a data scientist, and a local lawyer. They agreed that algorithms can help, but they also asked when human judgment should override a machine's recommendation. The panel's discussions were detailed and practical, focusing on real cases where automated decisions had affected residents. They wanted to ensure that efficiency did not come at the cost of fairness.

A. School admissions
In Riverton, a computer program now ranks students for oversubscribed schools. Last year, the program placed 72% of applicants in their first-choice school. This year, after the panel's review, the figure rose to 78%. The panel found that the program used distance from home as the main factor. However, it gave less weight to whether a child had a sibling at the school. Parents complained that this was unfair. The panel recommended that sibling priority should be added as a tie-breaker. The council accepted this change, and the new rule will start next September. This adjustment means that families with children already at a school will have a better chance of having siblings join them, reducing the disruption of attending different schools. The panel noted that such changes can improve equity without significantly affecting overall efficiency, as the program still processes applications quickly.

B. Traffic fines
Riverton uses cameras to detect speeding. In 2022, the system issued 12,000 fines. In 2023, the number fell to 9,500, a decrease of about 21%. The panel noted that the drop was partly because the city lowered the speed limit on two main roads. However, the cameras also made mistakes. About 3% of fines were sent to the wrong car owner. The panel said that a human should check every fine before it is sent. The council agreed to hire two more staff members to review the fines. The panel also suggested that drivers should be able to appeal online within 14 days, not 7 days as before. This extension gives drivers more time to respond, especially if they need to gather evidence or seek advice. The panel emphasized that human oversight is essential to maintain trust in the system. They argued that even a small error rate can undermine public confidence, so manual checks are a worthwhile investment.

C. Social housing
Riverton has a waiting list for social housing. The list is ordered by a points system. Points are given for factors such as income, family size, and time on the list. The panel found that the system gave more points to people who had lived in Riverton for a long time. This meant that newcomers waited longer. The panel argued that this was not fair to families who had recently moved to the city for work. They recommended that the time-on-list factor should be reduced from 40% to 25% of the total points. The council is still discussing this recommendation. No decision has been made yet. The panel noted that while rewarding long-term residency can build community stability, it can also disadvantage those who move for employment opportunities, which is a common pattern in a growing town. They suggested that other factors, such as current housing need, should be given more weight to reflect immediate circumstances.

D. The panel's conclusions
The panel published a short report. It said that algorithms are useful for handling large amounts of data quickly. However, they can hide unfair rules inside complex calculations. The report stated: 'An algorithm is only as fair as the rules we give it.' The panel recommended three general principles. First, every algorithm used in public services should be explained in simple language. Second, people affected by a decision should have the right to ask for a human review. Third, the city should check its algorithms every year. The council will vote on these principles in June. If they are accepted, Riverton will be the first town in the region to have such rules. These principles aim to make algorithmic decision-making more transparent and accountable, ensuring that citizens can understand and challenge automated outcomes. The panel stressed that transparency builds trust and allows for continuous improvement.

The panel also compared Riverton with the nearby town of Westfield. Westfield uses a similar school admissions program, but it does not use cameras for traffic fines. Instead, Westfield employs traffic officers. The panel found that Westfield's approach was more expensive but produced fewer mistakes. However, Westfield's system was slower. The panel concluded that there is no perfect system. Each town must balance speed, cost, and fairness. The ARG will meet again in September to review progress. The comparison highlighted that while automation can improve efficiency, it may introduce errors that human officers would avoid, and that the choice of system depends on local priorities and resources. The panel recommended that Riverton continue to evaluate its systems and learn from neighboring towns.

grammar.title: 趋势、比较、比例与数据句的准确性
grammar.explanation: 在描述数据时，我们常用不同的动词和结构来表达趋势、比较和比例。表示上升可用 rise, increase, go up；表示下降可用 fall, decrease, drop。注意时态：过去的数据用过去时（rose, fell），预测或未来安排用将来时（will start, will vote）。比较级用于两者比较：more expensive than, fewer mistakes than。比例常用百分比：72% of applicants, a decrease of about 21%。数据句要准确：数字、百分比、时间必须与事实一致。
grammar.example: This year, after the panel's review, the figure rose to 78%.

questions.explanation: next September表示将来，用will start。
questions.evidence: The council accepted this change, and the new rule will start next September.

questions.explanation: 2023是过去时间，用过去式fell。
questions.evidence: In 2023, the number fell to 9,500, a decrease of about 21%.

questions.explanation: 比较级用more expensive than。
questions.evidence: The panel found that Westfield's approach was more expensive but produced fewer mistakes.

questions.explanation: from...to...表示从……到……的变化。
questions.evidence: They recommended that the time-on-list factor should be reduced from 40% to 25% of the total points.

questions.explanation: 百分比后接of表示“……的百分之……”。
questions.evidence: About 3% of fines were sent to the wrong car owner.

questions.explanation: in June指将来，用will vote。
questions.evidence: The council will vote on these principles in June.

questions.explanation: mistakes是可数名词复数，比较级用fewer。
questions.evidence: The panel found that Westfield's approach was more expensive but produced fewer mistakes.

materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，不是官方雅思试题，也不代表任何官方分数。请先听/读对话，完成10道听力题；然后学习语法规则并完成8道语法题；最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。答案必须来自原文，填空答案须与原文完全一致。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Okay, everyone, thanks for coming. This is the weekly review panel for the city's new school-placement algorithm. We have three items: the data we used, the fairness checks, and the appeal process. Let's start with the data. Tomas, you looked at the numbers.

Tomas: Yes. The algorithm placed 12,400 students this year. That's about 8 percent more than last year, when it placed 11,500. The main reason is that the city grew. But here's the thing: the share of students who got their first-choice school fell from 71 percent to 64 percent. So more students, but fewer happy ones.

Maya: That's a big drop. Why?

Tomas: Two reasons. First, more students applied to the same popular schools. Second, we changed the tie-breaker. Last year, distance from home was the only tie-breaker. This year, we added a sibling rule: if an older brother or sister already attends the school, the younger child gets priority. That helped some families but made competition harder for others.

Priya: Can I jump in? I think the sibling rule is fair in principle, but it has an unintended effect. Families with more children get an advantage. A family with one child has no chance to use it. So the rule favors larger families. Is that what we want?

Tomas: That's a good point. But without the sibling rule, we had complaints from parents who wanted their children at the same school. It's a trade-off.

Maya: Let's park that for a moment and look at the fairness checks. Priya, you ran the audit.

Priya: Right. We checked outcomes by income group. For low-income students, the first-choice rate was 58 percent. For middle-income students, it was 66 percent. For high-income students, it was 72 percent. So there is a gap of 14 percentage points between the lowest and highest groups. Last year, the gap was 9 points. So the gap has widened.

Maya: That's concerning. Do we know why?

Priya: Partly because high-income families tend to live closer to popular schools, and distance still matters. Also, they have more resources to navigate the system. But I want to be careful: the algorithm itself doesn't use income. It uses distance, sibling status, and a random number. The gap comes from the inputs, not the code.

Tomas: That's an important distinction. The algorithm is neutral, but the data isn't.

Maya: Okay. Now the appeal process. How many appeals did we receive?

Priya: We received 430 appeals. Of those, 290 were about the sibling rule. The rest were about distance calculations. We resolved 380 appeals, and 50 are still open. The average resolution time was 11 days, down from 18 days last year. So we are faster, but we still have a backlog.

Maya: And what about the outcomes of the appeals? Did any students get a different school?

Priya: Yes. In 120 cases, we changed the placement. Most of those were due to data errors, like a wrong address. Only 15 were due to the sibling rule being applied incorrectly. So the system is mostly working, but errors happen.

Tomas: I'd like to add one more thing. We should compare this year's algorithm with the old paper-based system. The old system took about six weeks to produce results. The new one takes four days. That's a huge improvement in speed. But speed isn't everything. We need to make sure the faster system is also fair.

Maya: Agreed. So where does that leave us? We have more students, a lower first-choice rate, a wider income gap, and a faster but still imperfect appeal process. What should we recommend?

Priya: I suggest we keep the sibling rule but add a review after one year. And we should improve address data to reduce errors.

Tomas: I agree with the review. But I'd also like to see a simulation of what would happen if we removed the sibling rule. That would give us evidence.

Maya: Good. Let's summarize: we will recommend a one-year review of the sibling rule, a data-quality project for addresses, and a simulation of alternative rules. Any objections? No? Then we're done. Thanks, everyone.

grammar.title: 趋势、比较、比例、时态与数据句的准确性
grammar.explanation: 在描述数据时，先判断是“趋势变化”还是“静态比较”。趋势变化常用动词 rise/fall/increase/decrease，并搭配 from...to... 表示起点和终点；也可以用“has widened/narrowed”表示差距变化。比较两个数字时，用比较级（higher/lower/faster）或“compared with”。比例用 percent 或 percentage points：percent 表示比例本身，percentage points 表示两个百分比之间的差。时态要准确：过去的数据用一般过去时，当前状态用一般现在时，从过去到现在的变化可用现在完成时。数据句要避免歧义：数字后要说明对象，比较时要说明比较对象。

materials.title: How Scientific Disagreement Is Communicated
materials.instructions: 这是为B2–C1学习者设计的原创模拟阅读材料（非官方雅思材料）。请先阅读文章，然后完成10道题（单选、填空、匹配、判断）。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。建议先通读全文，再逐题作答。
materials.passage:
A. In the small coastal town of Marlow Bay, a dispute among scientists became public in an unusual way. Dr. Elena Torres, a marine biologist, claimed that the local seagrass beds were declining rapidly. Her evidence came from three years of underwater surveys. However, Dr. Samuel Reed, an environmental chemist, argued that the decline was seasonal, not permanent. He pointed to water samples collected each winter. The disagreement was not about facts alone; it was about how those facts were communicated to the public. This distinction matters because scientific evidence rarely speaks for itself. The same measurements can support different interpretations depending on when, where and how they are collected, and on how confidently those interpretations are presented to people who are not specialists. In other words, data do not automatically produce agreement; they must be explained, questioned and compared before a community can decide what they mean. This is especially true in small communities, where residents often know the scientists personally and may judge their claims as much by tone and manner as by the numbers themselves.

B. Torres first presented her findings at a town hall meeting. She used simple charts and avoided technical terms. "The seagrass is shrinking," she said. "We need to act now." Her presentation was clear, but some residents felt it was too alarming. Reed, who attended the meeting, responded a week later with a letter to the local newspaper. In his letter, he explained that seagrass naturally varies with seasons. He wrote, "The data are not yet conclusive." His tone was calm, but his message was less urgent. The contrast between the two styles was striking. Torres emphasised immediate risk, while Reed stressed patience and caution. Neither approach was dishonest, yet each left out part of the picture, and residents were left unsure whom to believe. The episode revealed how strongly tone, timing and choice of detail can shape public trust, even when both speakers are sincere. It also showed that a scientist who speaks first can set the terms of the debate, while a later reply may seem defensive even when it is reasonable.

C. The two scientists then agreed to a public debate, moderated by a science journalist. During the debate, Torres was asked about her data. She admitted that her surveys were mostly in summer. Reed was asked about his samples. He acknowledged that his winter data might miss summer changes. Both scientists were then invited to design a joint study. The audience was surprised by how quickly the disagreement turned into cooperation. What impressed people most was not that the scientists changed their minds, but that they were honest about the limits of their own evidence. By answering questions directly, each showed respect for the other's work and for the audience's intelligence. This honesty did not weaken their positions; instead, it made both of them more credible. Admitting uncertainty, they demonstrated, is not the same as admitting error, and the public responded well to that distinction.

D. The joint study was conducted over two years. Water temperature, light levels, and seagrass coverage were measured every month. The results showed that seagrass did decline in summer, but it recovered in winter. Both scientists were partly right. Torres's summer data were accurate, and Reed's winter observations were also correct. The full picture was more complex than either had claimed. Seasonal heat and light stress weakened the plants in the warmer months, while cooler conditions allowed them to grow back. Neither the rapid decline nor the seasonal pattern alone told the whole story; only the combined, year-round record did. The study therefore did more than settle an argument: it produced a clearer, more useful account of how the seagrass actually behaves. It also gave local officials a stronger basis for decisions about coastal protection, because the findings could be explained to the public in plain language.

E. How was this disagreement communicated so effectively? First, both scientists were willing to listen. Second, the debate was moderated fairly. Third, the joint study was designed before the debate ended. The town learned that scientific disagreement is not a failure; it is a normal part of research. When communicated openly, it can lead to better understanding. The episode also showed that a fair moderator and a shared plan can turn a public argument into a shared investigation, giving citizens a model for judging competing claims rather than simply choosing sides. Such a model is valuable well beyond Marlow Bay, because public debates about science are common and often confusing. Citizens who learn to ask about methods, timing and evidence are better prepared to take part in them.

F. Today, Marlow Bay has a new sign at the beach. It reads: "Seagrass changes with seasons. Science works best when we listen to each other." The sign was designed by local students. The story of Torres and Reed is now used in schools to teach how scientists can disagree and still work together. Teachers use the case to show that evidence, communication and cooperation are equally important, and that a dispute handled well can leave a community better informed than before.

grammar.title: 被动语态、顺序、地点、变化及句子间衔接
grammar.explanation: 本课重点：1) 被动语态（be + 过去分词）强调动作承受者，如“The sign was designed by local students.”；2) 顺序（first, second, third）使说明有条理；3) 地点介词（at, in, on）表示位置；4) 变化动词（decline, recover, vary）描述趋势；5) 句子间衔接（however, therefore, then）使逻辑连贯。

materials.title: How Scientific Disagreement Is Communicated
materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，非官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。请先听/读英文材料，再完成10道听力理解题（题型混合：单选、填空、匹配、判断正误/未提及）。填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。之后学习语法点（被动语态、顺序、地点、变化及句子间衔接），完成8道新句语法题。最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Welcome back to Science Weekly. I'm Maya Chen. Today we're talking about how scientists disagree—and how they communicate that disagreement to the public. With me is Dr. Leo Park, a science communication researcher. Leo, thanks for joining.
Leo: Thanks, Maya. Happy to be here.
Maya: So, first, what does scientific disagreement actually look like? Is it like a big argument?
Leo: Not usually. Most disagreement happens in papers, at conferences, and in peer review. It's formal and slow. For example, one team publishes a result, and another team tries to repeat it. If the second team gets a different result, they write a comment. Then the first team replies. It can take months.
Maya: Months? That's slow.
Leo: Yes, but that's the point. The process is designed to be careful. It's not a fight; it's a check.
Maya: But the public often sees it as a fight. Why?
Leo: Because the media likes conflict. A headline like "Scientists disagree!" gets clicks. But the actual disagreement is often narrow. Two groups might agree on 90 percent of the data and disagree on one small point. The public sees the 10 percent.
Maya: So how should scientists talk about this? What's the best way?
Leo: First, they should be clear about what is known and what is uncertain. Second, they should explain the process. Say: "This is how we check results." Third, they should avoid saying "the science is settled" when it isn't. That phrase makes people distrust scientists later.
Maya: Interesting. Can you give an example of a disagreement that was communicated well?
Leo: Sure. A few years ago, two teams disagreed about the age of a rock formation. One team said 200 million years; the other said 210 million. They published a joint statement. They said: "We agree on the method. We disagree on one measurement. We are working together to resolve it." The public understood. Trust stayed high.
Maya: That's a good model. What about a bad example?
Leo: A bad example is when scientists attack each other personally on social media. That makes the public think the whole field is unreliable. It's better to criticize the idea, not the person.
Maya: So the rule is: disagree with the idea, not the person?
Leo: Exactly. And always explain the evidence. If you say "my colleague is wrong," that's not enough. You must say why.
Maya: What about uncertainty? Scientists often say "more research is needed." Does that confuse people?
Leo: It can. But it's honest. The problem is when scientists say it without context. A better sentence is: "We are 80 percent confident in this result, and we need one more study to be sure." That gives people a number and a reason.
Maya: So numbers help?
Leo: Numbers help when they are explained. A number alone can scare people. "A 10 percent risk" sounds big. But "10 out of 100 people" is clearer.
Maya: Let's talk about the order of information. Does order matter?
Leo: Yes. Start with what you agree on. Then state the disagreement. Then explain the next step. That order builds trust. If you start with the conflict, people stop listening.
Maya: So: agreement, disagreement, next step.
Leo: Exactly. And use clear linking words: "however," "therefore," "in addition." These words show the logic.
Maya: What about place? Does location matter—where the disagreement happens?
Leo: It can. A disagreement in a private email is different from one in a public journal. Public disagreements are seen by everyone, so they must be more careful. Private ones can be more direct.
Maya: And change over time? How do disagreements end?
Leo: They end when new data arrives. Sometimes one side changes its mind. That's a success, not a failure. But the public often sees a change of mind as weakness. We need to reframe that: changing your mind when evidence changes is good science.
Maya: So the message is: disagreement is normal, and it can be healthy.
Leo: Yes. The goal is not to hide disagreement. The goal is to explain it clearly. If the public sees the process, they trust the result more.
Maya: Leo, thank you. That was very clear.
Leo: Thank you, Maya.

materials.title: The Uncertainty Seminar: Evaluating Public Claims
materials.instructions: 阅读以下模拟教育材料（非官方雅思测试）。先通读文章，理解大意；再完成10道题（单选、填空、判断正误/未提及）。填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。注意：本材料为原创模拟内容，不涉及真实研究或引用。
materials.passage:
A seminar on uncertainty in public claims was held last week at a community learning centre. The event was organised by a local group called Clear Thinking and was attended by about forty adults. The seminar was designed to help people evaluate claims they see in news reports, advertisements, and social media. The main speaker was Dr. Elena Marsh, a science communicator who has worked with several public health campaigns. The seminar was divided into three parts: a presentation, a group exercise, and a final discussion.

In the first part, Dr. Marsh explained why uncertainty is often hidden in public messages. She said that many claims are presented as certain when they are actually based on limited evidence. For example, a food product might be advertised as “proven to improve memory,” but the study behind it might have involved only twenty people. Dr. Marsh emphasised that the size of a study matters, and so does the way it was conducted. She also introduced the idea of “confidence levels,” which show how sure researchers are about their results. A confidence level of 95% does not mean there is a 95% chance the claim is true; it means that if the study were repeated many times, 95% of the results would fall within a certain range. This distinction was new to most participants. Dr. Marsh added that uncertainty is not a sign of bad science; rather, it is an honest reflection of what research can and cannot tell us. She noted that public messages often remove uncertainty to make claims sound more convincing, which can mislead people. For instance, advertisers may highlight a single positive result while ignoring the broader context of the research. This selective presentation can create a false sense of certainty and lead consumers to make poorly informed decisions. To illustrate further, she mentioned that even well-designed studies can have limitations, such as small sample sizes or confounding factors, and that acknowledging these limitations is part of responsible reporting. She explained that confounding factors are additional influences that researchers may not have controlled, and these can distort the apparent link between cause and effect. Recognising such details helps readers judge whether a claim is as strong as it first appears.

After the presentation, the participants were given a group exercise. They were divided into small groups and each group was given a short news article to analyse. The articles had been chosen to include different types of uncertainty. One group was asked to identify the source of a claim about a new diet. Another group had to find out whether a statistic about crime rates was based on a national survey or a local one. A third group was asked to check if a claim about a medicine had been approved by a regulatory agency. The groups were told to mark any sentences where uncertainty was not clearly stated. After twenty minutes, each group presented its findings. Many participants said they had not noticed the missing uncertainty before the exercise. The exercise helped them see how easily uncertainty can be overlooked when reading quickly. It also demonstrated that even seemingly straightforward articles can contain hidden assumptions or gaps in evidence.

In the final discussion, Dr. Marsh answered questions from the audience. One participant asked how ordinary people can check claims without special knowledge. Dr. Marsh suggested three simple steps: first, look for the original source of the claim; second, check whether the source is independent; and third, see if other reliable sources report the same thing. She warned that headlines are often written to attract attention, so they may exaggerate or simplify the findings. Another participant asked about the role of social media algorithms. Dr. Marsh explained that algorithms are designed to show content that keeps people engaged, which can mean that uncertain claims are repeated more often than careful corrections. She recommended that people follow a variety of sources and be cautious of claims that promise quick fixes. She also advised checking the date of the information, as old studies may no longer be relevant. In addition, she pointed out that algorithms can create echo chambers, where users mainly see information that confirms their existing beliefs, making it harder to encounter balanced perspectives. She suggested that users actively seek out opposing viewpoints and verify information through fact-checking websites. She added that this habit of checking several sources takes little time once it becomes routine, and it can greatly reduce the chance of being misled by a single dramatic headline.

The seminar ended with a short evaluation form. Participants were asked to rate the usefulness of the session and to suggest topics for future events. Most feedback was positive, and several people requested a follow-up seminar on how to read scientific studies. Clear Thinking plans to run a similar event next month, focusing on claims about climate and health. The organisers said that the seminar would be repeated in a larger venue because demand had been higher than expected. They also noted that the materials used in the exercise would be made available online after the event.

materials.transcript:
Maya: Welcome, everyone. Today we're looking at how public claims are evaluated when the evidence is uncertain. Let's start with a claim that was made last month: 'The new park will reduce city temperatures by two degrees.'

Ben: Sorry, can I just check — was that two degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit?

Maya: Good question. The original report said two degrees Celsius, but it was later corrected to one degree. So the claim was revised.

Ben: Right. And was the measurement taken in summer or winter?

Maya: It was taken in summer, over three weeks. But the sample was small — only one neighborhood.

Ben: So the claim is uncertain because the data is limited.

Maya: Exactly. Now, how should we present this to the public? We need to be clear about what is known and what is not.

Ben: I think we should say: 'Early results suggest a small cooling effect, but more data is needed.'

Maya: That's better. It avoids overclaiming. Now let's look at the second claim: 'The new bus route has reduced traffic by 30 percent.'

Ben: Was that measured before and after the route opened?

Maya: Yes, but only on one road. And the measurement was taken during a holiday period, so traffic was already low.

Ben: So the 30 percent figure might be misleading.

Maya: Correct. The claim was based on a short period and a single location. Now, what about the third claim: 'The library will be closed for renovation next month.'

Ben: That one seems clear. Was there an official announcement?

Maya: Yes, the city council announced it. But the exact dates were not given.

Ben: So the claim is true, but the details are incomplete.

Maya: Right. Now, let's think about how to communicate uncertainty. We can use phrases like 'it is likely that', 'the evidence suggests', or 'further research is needed'.

Ben: And we should avoid saying 'it is proven' when it isn't.

Maya: Exactly. Also, when we describe a process, we should use the passive voice to focus on the action, not the person. For example: 'The data was collected over three weeks.'

Ben: And for sequences, we use words like 'first', 'then', 'after that', 'finally'.

Maya: Yes. And for changes, we can say 'the temperature increased by one degree' or 'traffic decreased from 100 to 70 vehicles per hour'.

Ben: What about linking ideas between sentences? We can use 'however', 'therefore', 'in addition'.

Maya: Good. Now, let's practice with a short example. Imagine a claim: 'The new lighting in the park has reduced crime by 15 percent.'

Ben: Was that measured over a full year?

Maya: No, only six months. And the police reports were incomplete.

Ben: So the claim is uncertain. We should say: 'Initial data suggests a possible reduction, but the evidence is limited.'

Maya: Perfect. Now, let's review the key points. First, check the source of the data. Second, check the time period. Third, check the location. Finally, check if the claim has been revised.

Ben: And always use cautious language when the evidence is uncertain.

Maya: Exactly. That's all for today. Thank you.

materials.title: The River Cleanup Debate: Policy at Three Scales
materials.instructions: 项目原创模拟场景与数据，不是官方试卷。阅读文章后独立回答10题，再检查逐题依据。题目包含信息定位、论证范围、比较及推断；遇到词汇可用划词帮助，但使用帮助不算独立测评。语法先看规则，再做新语境练习。
materials.passage:
A
In the imaginary town of Riverton, the local council proposed a new policy to clean up the Green River. The plan, called the River Health Initiative, would require factories along the river to reduce their waste by 30 percent within two years. The council argued that the river's water quality had fallen sharply over the past decade, and that fish populations had dropped by nearly half. They pointed to a recent survey showing that 70 percent of residents supported stricter rules. This suggested that public opinion was strongly in favour of action, giving the council a mandate to act. However, the plan also faced opposition. Small business owners warned that the cost of new equipment could force them to close, and some scientists noted that the survey had only interviewed 200 people. A sample of that size, they argued, might not accurately represent the views of the whole town. The debate quickly moved beyond Riverton, raising questions about how environmental policy should work at different levels.

B
At the national level, the government had already set a target: all rivers should be clean enough for swimming by 2035. To achieve this, it offered funding to towns that adopted strict waste limits. But the national rules were general, and they did not specify how each town should meet them. This created a problem. Riverton's council wanted to use the national funding to build a new water treatment plant, but the national government required towns to show 'measurable progress' within one year. Since building a plant would take at least three years, Riverton could not meet that condition. As a result, the town had to look for other solutions, such as asking factories to pay for smaller, quicker upgrades. The national policy, though well-intentioned, did not fit the local timeline. This mismatch between national ambitions and local realities is a common challenge in environmental governance. It shows that even well-designed national policies can fail when they ignore the practical constraints faced by local communities. Local governments often have limited budgets and staff, and they may lack the technical expertise to meet complex national requirements. Without flexibility, towns like Riverton are left struggling to comply, which can delay progress and frustrate both officials and residents. Such delays can also erode public trust, making future environmental initiatives harder to launch. To address this, national governments could offer phased deadlines or provide technical support, allowing local areas to adapt policies to their own circumstances.

C
Meanwhile, a regional environmental group proposed a different approach. They suggested that instead of punishing factories, the town could create a 'clean river fund' financed by a small tax on all businesses. The fund would pay for regular water testing and for helping factories buy better equipment. The group argued that this method would be fairer, because even businesses that did not pollute directly would contribute to the river's health. They also claimed that it would be more effective, since factories would have support rather than penalties. However, critics pointed out that the tax might discourage new businesses from opening in Riverton, and that the fund could be mismanaged. The debate showed that even a simple goal—clean water—can be pursued in very different ways depending on who is making the decision. It also highlighted the tension between collective responsibility and economic competitiveness. Supporters of the fund argued that a shared financial burden would build a sense of common purpose, while opponents feared that extra costs would drive investment to neighbouring towns with lower taxes. Such trade-offs are typical in environmental policy, where economic and ecological goals often pull in different directions. Finding a balance requires open discussion and a willingness to compromise.

The council also asked how any improvement would be evaluated. Testing only beside upgraded factories could make the scheme appear more successful than it was across the entire river. An independent team therefore proposed fixed sampling points upstream and downstream, measurements in both wet and dry seasons, and publication of the sampling procedure before the programme began. These steps would not prove that every change resulted from the policy: rainfall and waste arriving from outside the town could still affect the readings. They would, however, make selective reporting harder and allow later results to be compared with a credible baseline. A headline percentage without those conditions would be a weaker basis for further investment.

D
What can we learn from this simulated case? First, policies designed at one level may not work smoothly at another. National targets can be too broad, while local plans may lack resources. Second, the choice between punishment and support is not always clear-cut. A policy that seems fair to some may seem unfair to others. Third, public opinion matters, but it must be measured carefully; a small survey can be misleading. Finally, timelines are crucial. A plan that promises quick results may fail if the necessary infrastructure takes years to build. In the end, the best policy may be one that combines national funding, local flexibility, and fair contributions from all businesses. The River Health Initiative may not have been perfect, but the debate it sparked was a valuable lesson in how environmental policy works across different scales. It reminds us that environmental problems are rarely solved by simple solutions; they require ongoing dialogue, careful planning, and a willingness to adapt when circumstances change.

grammar.title: 让步、条件、因果：复杂句与简单句的清楚组合
grammar.explanation: 让步承认一个事实但指出预期结果未发生，例如原句though well-intentioned承认政策出发点好，却不能解决地方期限问题。完整让步从句用although/though + 主语 + 谓语；同一主语的be有时可省略。despite是介词，接名词或-ing，不能直接接完整从句。because引原因、so/therefore引结果，不能不顾实际逻辑互换。unless表示if not；only if表示必要条件而不是保证结果。正式论证还要区分may（可能）与must（必要/强推断），避免把证据写得过强。
grammar.example: The national policy, though well-intentioned, did not fit the local timeline.

questions.prompt: The town considers good intentions a positive point, but says they did not solve the timing problem. Choose the concessive linker: ___ the intentions were good, the timetable remained impractical.

questions.evidence: The town considers good intentions a positive point, but says they did not solve the timing problem. Choose the concessive linker: Although the intentions were good, the timetable remained impractical.

questions.prompt: Preserve the stated condition: If you do not study harder, you will fail the exam. You will fail the exam ___ you study harder.

questions.evidence: Express the stated result, not a reason for being tired: She was tired, so she went to bed early.

materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，不是官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。请先听/读全文，再完成10道题。听力部分注意不同说话人之间的自然接话与修正；阅读部分注意段落A/B/C。语法部分先用中文理解“让步、条件、因果”的表达，再完成8道新句子的选择题。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Okay, everyone, thanks for coming. This is the Riverbend town council's informal session on the proposed plastic bag fee. I'm Maya, the council's policy analyst. Let's start with the town level. If we introduce a five-cent fee per bag, we expect shops to reduce bag use by about thirty percent in the first year. That's a conditional claim, not a promise.

Daniel: Sorry, Maya, can I push back on that? Thirty percent sounds high. In other towns, the drop was closer to fifteen percent. So unless we add a public information campaign, I doubt we'll hit thirty.

Maya: Fair point, Daniel. Let me correct myself. The thirty percent figure assumes a campaign. Without one, fifteen percent is more realistic. So the condition matters.

Priya: I'm Priya from the Riverbend Retail Association. Even if the fee is small, our members worry about paperwork. Although the fee is only five cents, the reporting form is two pages long. That's a burden for small shops, especially those with limited staff and resources.

Maya: That's a valid concern. We could simplify the form. If the form is one page, compliance should improve. And because small shops have fewer staff, a simple form helps them most. We should also consider offering online submission to reduce administrative work.

Daniel: But what about the regional level? The county wants a uniform rule. If Riverbend acts alone, shoppers may drive to the next town to avoid the fee. That's leakage. And leakage means we lose both revenue and environmental benefits.

Priya: Exactly. So even though a town fee is popular, a county-wide rule would be more effective. Although it's harder to pass, it closes the leakage gap. Our members would rather have one consistent rule across the county than a patchwork of local fees.

Maya: Right. So the town fee works only if neighboring towns cooperate. Otherwise, the environmental gain is smaller than we hope. We should coordinate with county officials to align our timelines.

Daniel: And the state level? The state is considering a ban on thin plastic bags altogether. If the state bans them, the town fee becomes irrelevant for those bags. But a ban would also require enforcement and public education.

Maya: True. But a state ban takes two years. So in the short term, the town fee still matters. Because the state timeline is slow, local action fills the gap. We can also use the town fee as a pilot to inform state policy.

Priya: Our members would accept a town fee if the state ban is coming. They prefer one clear rule to three confusing ones. Although they dislike fees, they dislike uncertainty more. A clear timeline from the state would help them plan.

Maya: Good. So here's the summary. The town fee reduces bags only if we run a campaign and simplify the form. The county rule is stronger because it prevents leakage. The state ban is the cleanest, but it is slow. Since each scale has a different speed, we should act at the town level now and support the county and state plans. This layered approach ensures we make progress while avoiding confusion.

Daniel: One more correction. Earlier I said fifteen percent without a campaign. Actually, the study said twelve percent. So twelve, not fifteen. I apologize for the error.

Maya: Thanks, Daniel. Twelve percent without a campaign, thirty with one. Let's note that. Any final questions? No? Then we'll draft the proposal. Thanks, everyone.

materials.title: The Ripple Effect: When a Well-Meant Rule Backfires
materials.instructions: 阅读下面的文章（约900词），完成10道题。文章为模拟教学材料，非真实事件。注意：题目中的选项均为完整英文句子；填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。语法部分先学习中文讲解，再完成8道新句子的练习。
materials.passage:
In the small coastal town of Marlow Bay, the local council introduced a policy in 2022 to reduce plastic waste. The policy required all food stalls in the weekly market to use only compostable containers. The council believed this would cut landfill waste by 40 percent within a year. At first, the plan seemed successful: within three months, the amount of plastic waste from the market dropped by 35 percent. However, a closer look revealed unexpected problems. Many stallholders, unable to afford the higher cost of compostable containers, simply stopped selling hot food. As a result, the market's overall waste decreased, but so did its revenue and visitor numbers. The council had achieved its environmental target, but at the cost of damaging the local economy. This outcome shows how a narrow focus on one environmental indicator can obscure broader social and economic effects. The stallholders were not acting out of disregard for the environment; they were responding rationally to a rule that ignored their financial reality. When compliance becomes too expensive, people often withdraw from the activity altogether rather than absorb the cost. In this case, the council measured success by the weight of plastic collected, but it failed to ask whether the market could still function as a place of business. The result was a cleaner market that was also a quieter and poorer one.

A similar story unfolded at Greenfield School. To improve student health, the school banned all sugary drinks from its canteen. The head teacher announced that students would only be allowed water or milk. The ban was popular with parents, and within a term, the school saw a 20 percent drop in students buying drinks at lunch. But teachers soon noticed that some students were bringing large bottles of soda from home and drinking them secretly. Others started buying sugary drinks from a nearby shop before school. The policy had reduced the school's official sales figures, but it had not changed students' actual consumption. In fact, the school nurse reported a slight increase in students feeling tired in the afternoon, possibly because they were replacing balanced meals with sugary snacks from outside. Thus, the school's measure of success—canteen sales—did not reflect real dietary habits. The rule changed the location of the behaviour rather than the behaviour itself, and the official statistics gave a misleading impression of progress. Parents who supported the ban were often unaware that their children were simply finding sugar elsewhere, which meant the school's apparent victory was largely an illusion created by its own accounting.

These examples illustrate a common problem in policy design: unintended consequences. When policymakers focus on a single measurable target, they may overlook how people will adapt their behaviour. In Marlow Bay, the target was plastic reduction; in Greenfield, it was sugar reduction. In both cases, the policy changed what was measured, but not necessarily what mattered. Economists call this 'Goodhart's Law': when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The council and the school both achieved their numerical goals, yet the underlying issues remained or even worsened. Such gaps between official figures and real-world outcomes are a warning sign for anyone designing rules based on a single indicator. The danger is not that the numbers are false, but that they capture only a narrow slice of reality while the wider picture moves in the opposite direction. A policy can look like a triumph in a monthly report while quietly making life harder for the very people it was meant to help.

So how can policymakers avoid such traps? First, they should consult the people affected before implementing a rule. Stallholders could have suggested a subsidy for compostable containers, and students could have been involved in designing a healthier canteen menu. Second, policies should include multiple indicators, not just one. For example, Marlow Bay could have tracked both plastic waste and market revenue. Third, regular review is essential. A policy that looks good on paper may fail in practice, and adjustments should be made quickly. Finally, communication matters: if people understand the reason for a rule, they are more likely to follow it willingly rather than find ways around it. These steps help ensure that a policy's success is measured in ways that reflect genuine improvement, not just convenient numbers. Consultation also builds trust, which makes future policies easier to introduce and more likely to be accepted. When people feel their concerns have been heard, they are less likely to resist a rule and more likely to suggest practical solutions that policymakers might never have considered on their own.

Of course, not all policies have negative side effects. Some well-designed rules achieve their goals without causing harm. But the Marlow Bay and Greenfield cases remind us that good intentions are not enough. Careful planning, broad consultation, and flexible evaluation are needed to turn a well-meant idea into effective action. As one council member in Marlow Bay put it, 'We learned that you can't just look at the numbers on a report; you have to look at the people behind them.'

grammar.title: 让步、条件与因果：复杂句和简单句的清楚组合
grammar.explanation: 在英语中，我们可以用不同的连接词来表达让步（虽然、尽管）、条件（如果、除非）和因果（因为、所以）。让步常用 although, though, even though, while 等；条件常用 if, unless, as long as 等；因果常用 because, since, as, so, therefore 等。复杂句可以包含一个主句和一个或多个从句，而简单句只包含一个主谓结构。写作时，交替使用复杂句和简单句可以使文章节奏更好、逻辑更清晰。例如：'Although the policy was popular, it had unintended effects.'（让步）'If people understand the reason, they are more likely to follow.'（条件）'The council achieved its target, but it damaged the economy.'（转折/因果）。注意：although 和 but 不能同时用在同一个句子中；because 和 so 也不能同时使用。
grammar.example: Although the policy was popular with parents, the school saw a 20 percent drop in students buying drinks at lunch.

materials.title: The Ripple Effect: When Well-Meant Rules Backfire
materials.instructions: 本材料为模拟教学练习，并非官方雅思考试。请先听/读英文讲座，理解政策意外后果的逻辑。然后完成10道听力/阅读题（单选、填空、匹配、判断）。之后学习语法点“让步、条件、因果的清晰组合”，并完成8道新句语法题。最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。所有题目选项为英文，解释为中文。
materials.transcript:
Professor Lin: Good morning, everyone. Today we look at unintended policy consequences. Let me start with a small example. A city council wanted to reduce traffic downtown. So they built a new ring road around the city center. The road was wide and fast. Drivers loved it. But within two years, traffic downtown increased by fifteen percent. Why? Because the new road made driving into the city easier. More people decided to drive. This is called induced demand. Although the council built the road to reduce traffic, it actually attracted more cars. 

Student A: Professor, does that mean we should never build new roads? 

Professor Lin: Not exactly. We need to think about conditions. If a city builds new roads but also improves public transport, then the result may be different. The key is to combine policies. 

Student B: I read about a similar case with plastic bags. A government banned free plastic bags in supermarkets. Shoppers had to pay for them. At first, plastic bag use dropped by eighty percent. But then people started buying thicker, reusable bags. Those bags were made of more plastic. So total plastic production went up. The policy reduced one problem but created another. 

Professor Lin: Excellent example. This shows a trade-off. When you make one behavior costly, people may switch to another behavior that is also harmful. 

Student C: What about the tax on sugary drinks? Some cities tried that. 

Professor Lin: Yes. A tax on sugary drinks can reduce consumption. However, if the tax is too high, people may buy cheaper, unhealthy alternatives, like energy drinks with even more sugar. So the effect depends on how people respond. 

Student A: So policies always have side effects? 

Professor Lin: Almost always. But we can predict some of them. We use models. A model is a simplified picture of reality. It helps us ask: if we do X, what else might happen? For example, a rent control policy sets a maximum rent. It helps current tenants pay less. But if landlords cannot earn enough, they may stop renting out apartments. Then the supply of housing falls. In the long run, rent control can make housing harder to find. 

Student B: That sounds unfair. 

Professor Lin: It is a dilemma. The policy helps some people now but may hurt others later. Good policy design tries to balance short-term help with long-term effects. 

Student C: How do we know if a policy worked? 

Professor Lin: We compare what happened with what would have happened without the policy. That is called a counterfactual. It is hard because we cannot see the alternative world. But we can use data from similar cities. 

Student A: So the main lesson is to think carefully before we act? 

Professor Lin: Yes. And to monitor results after we act. Policies are experiments. We must be ready to adjust them. 

Student B: Thank you, Professor. This was very clear. 

Professor Lin: You're welcome. Next week we will discuss how to communicate policy changes to the public.

materials.title: The Dashboard Dilemma: Rethinking Workplace Culture and Measurement
materials.instructions: 阅读下面的文章，完成10个题目。文章是关于职场文化与结果衡量的原创模拟材料，不是真实事件。题目包括单选、填空、匹配（以单选形式）和判断正误（True/False/Not Given）。填空答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。请先通读全文，再作答。
materials.passage:
A
In the modern workplace, the pressure to measure outcomes is intense. Companies track sales figures, customer satisfaction scores, and project completion rates. These metrics offer a sense of control and clarity. However, an overemphasis on measurable results can create a toxic culture. When employees feel that only numbers matter, they may cut corners or hide problems. For example, a sales team might push customers into unwanted purchases to meet a target. This behavior damages trust and long-term relationships. Therefore, organizations need to balance outcome measurement with attention to process and employee well-being. A healthy culture requires leaders to recognize that not everything valuable can be easily counted. Trust, creativity, and teamwork are essential but difficult to quantify. When managers focus only on what can be measured, they may unintentionally discourage these important qualities. For instance, an employee who takes time to help a colleague solve a problem may not produce immediate measurable results, but their contribution strengthens the team in the long run. Thus, a narrow focus on metrics can undermine the very foundations of a productive workplace. This does not mean that measurement is inherently bad; rather, it means that measurement must be used thoughtfully. Metrics can highlight areas for improvement and help leaders make informed decisions. But when metrics become the only language of success, employees may feel reduced to numbers, and their motivation may suffer. A more balanced approach recognizes that quantitative data and qualitative experience together provide a fuller picture of organizational health.

B
One alternative is to use a balanced scorecard that includes both quantitative and qualitative indicators. Qualitative indicators, such as employee feedback and teamwork quality, are harder to measure but crucial for a healthy culture. If managers regularly ask for anonymous feedback, they can identify issues before they become crises. Moreover, when teams are rewarded for collaboration rather than individual competition, they tend to share knowledge and support each other. This shift does not mean abandoning metrics entirely; rather, it means using them as tools for improvement, not as weapons for punishment. For example, a company might set targets for both sales and customer retention, while also tracking how well departments communicate. By giving weight to qualitative factors, organizations signal that how results are achieved matters as much as the results themselves. This approach encourages employees to think about the long-term impact of their actions, not just short-term gains. It also fosters a sense of psychological safety, where employees feel safe to raise concerns and suggest improvements without fear of blame. When people believe that their voices are heard and that their well-being is valued, they are more likely to engage fully and contribute creatively. Over time, this can lead to stronger commitment and lower turnover, as employees see that the organization cares about more than just the bottom line.

C
Another approach is to focus on leading indicators instead of lagging ones. Lagging indicators, like quarterly profits, tell you what has already happened. Leading indicators, such as employee engagement levels or the number of innovative ideas submitted, predict future performance. By monitoring leading indicators, companies can intervene early and foster a culture of continuous learning. For instance, if a department shows a decline in engagement, managers can investigate workload or recognition issues before they affect output. This proactive stance contrasts with the reactive blame game that often follows poor lagging results. Leading indicators also help organizations adapt to change more quickly. In a fast-moving market, waiting for quarterly results to reveal problems may be too late. By paying attention to early warning signs, such as rising absenteeism or a drop in participation in team meetings, managers can address issues promptly. This forward-looking perspective supports a healthier, more resilient workplace. It encourages managers to ask questions rather than assign blame, and it helps employees feel that their daily experiences are taken seriously. When leading indicators are tracked consistently, they can become a normal part of management discussions, reducing the shock of negative surprises and building a culture of transparency and trust.

D
However, implementing these ideas is not without challenges. Employees may distrust new measurement systems if they suspect they are just another way to monitor them. Transparency is essential: workers need to understand why data is collected and how it will be used. Additionally, leaders must model the behavior they expect. If executives only talk about profits, employees will follow suit, regardless of official policies. Therefore, cultural change requires consistent effort and clear communication from the top. Leaders should explain the purpose of new metrics and involve employees in designing them. When people have a say in how they are measured, they are more likely to accept the system as fair. Training managers to use data for support rather than surveillance also builds trust. Without these steps, even well-intentioned measurement systems can backfire, creating suspicion and resistance. It is also important to acknowledge that change takes time. Employees may need repeated reassurance and visible evidence that new systems are not simply old controls in disguise. Leaders who listen to concerns and adjust their approach accordingly are more likely to gain genuine buy-in. Ultimately, the success of any measurement system depends on whether employees perceive it as a tool for growth or a threat to their autonomy.

E
In conclusion, while measuring outcomes is necessary, it should not come at the expense of workplace culture. A balanced approach that combines quantitative and qualitative measures, emphasizes leading indicators, and maintains transparency can create an environment where both people and performance thrive. Organizations that ignore this balance risk short-term gains at the cost of long-term success. By valuing process, well-being, and open communication alongside results, companies can build a culture that sustains high performance over time. The key is to see measurement as a tool for learning and improvement, not as a weapon for control or punishment.

materials.transcript:
Maya: Hi, Tom. You look worried. What's going on?
Tom: It's the new performance system. My manager, Rachel, wants us to log every task we do. She says it will help us measure outcomes better.
Maya: That sounds reasonable. What's the problem?
Tom: The problem is that we spend more time logging than working. Yesterday I spent forty minutes filling in a form about a ten-minute phone call.
Maya: Oh, I see. So the measurement itself is slowing you down.
Tom: Exactly. And because we're all busy logging, we've stopped helping each other. Last week, I didn't help a new colleague because I was behind on my log.
Maya: That's a real cost. But if you don't measure anything, how do you know what's working?
Tom: I agree we need some measurement. But the current system only counts quantity, not quality. For example, it counts how many calls we make, not how well we solve problems.
Maya: So the numbers don't show the full picture.
Tom: Right. And there's another issue. The system compares teams, so people hide problems to look good. If a team admits a mistake, they get a lower score.
Maya: That's dangerous. It encourages people to hide errors instead of fixing them.
Tom: Yes. And the worst part is that Rachel doesn't see this. She only looks at the dashboard.
Maya: Have you talked to her about it?
Tom: I tried. But she said the system is fair because everyone is measured the same way.
Maya: Hmm. That's a common argument, but it's not quite right. Measuring everyone the same way doesn't mean the measurement is fair if the work is different. For instance, if one team handles complex cases and another handles simple ones, the same metrics can't capture that difference fairly. Fairness in measurement depends on whether the metrics reflect the actual demands of the job.
Tom: That's a good point. I hadn't thought of it that way.
Maya: What if you suggested a small change? For instance, add a quality check to the system, or ask for a monthly team discussion about what the numbers miss.
Tom: That could work. But I'm not sure Rachel will listen. She's under pressure from senior management.
Maya: Maybe you could frame it as a way to improve the system, not as a criticism. If you show her that the current system hides problems, she might be more open.
Tom: So instead of saying "the system is bad," I could say "here's how to make it better."
Maya: Exactly. And you could bring examples from your team. Real stories are more convincing than opinions.
Tom: OK. I'll prepare a short document with two or three examples. But what if she still says no?
Maya: Then at least you've raised the issue. And you could ask for a trial period for the new idea. A trial is less threatening than a permanent change.
Tom: That makes sense. I feel better already. Thanks, Maya.
Maya: No problem. Let me know how it goes.

grammar.title: 因果关系、条件和对比；段落间逻辑与指代
grammar.explanation: 本课重点：1) 因果：because, so, that's why 等连接原因和结果；2) 条件：if 引导条件句，主句用情态动词或将来时；3) 对比：but, however, instead of, rather than 表示转折或替代；4) 段落间逻辑与指代：用 this, that, these, those, it, they 指代前文内容，使段落连贯。注意：if 从句用一般现在时，主句用 will/might/can 等。
grammar.example: If a team admits a mistake, they get a lower score.

questions.explanation: 前后为因果关系，前因后果用 so。

materials.title: The Participation Rate Puzzle
materials.instructions: 阅读一篇关于教育研究中“参与率”指标的模拟讨论（所有数据与场景均为原创模拟材料，非真实研究）。先理解文章，再完成10道题。注意：填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。语法部分先阅读中文讲解，再完成8道新句练习题。
materials.passage:
A
In the small coastal town of Marlow Bay, a regional education board has been using a single number to judge its after-school science clubs: the participation rate. This figure is calculated by dividing the number of students who attend at least one session by the total number of students enrolled in the district. For three years, the board has reported that participation is rising, and last spring it announced that the rate had reached 68 percent. The announcement was met with applause at a public meeting. However, a group of teachers and two local researchers have now challenged this common metric. They argue that the participation rate hides as much as it reveals, and that the board should adopt a more detailed set of measures that captures not only how many students take part but also how deeply they engage.

B
The challenge began when a teacher named Elena Ruiz noticed something odd. Although the participation rate was climbing, the number of students who attended ten or more sessions had fallen sharply. In other words, more students were trying the clubs once, but fewer were staying. “If a student comes to one session and never returns, we count that as a success,” Ruiz said at a staff meeting. “That does not match what we see in the classroom.” She and her colleague Dr. Samir Haddad, a researcher at a nearby university, decided to examine the club records in detail. They found that the average number of sessions attended per student had dropped from 6.2 to 3.8 over the same three-year period. The participation rate, they concluded, was measuring breadth but not depth. A club could therefore appear healthy on paper while, in practice, offering little sustained experience to most of its members.

C
The board’s initial response was defensive. A board member, Priya Nair, pointed out that the participation rate is simple to understand and cheap to collect. “Parents and politicians can grasp it immediately,” she said. “If we replace it with a complicated index, we may lose public support.” Haddad agreed that simplicity has value, but he argued that a misleading simple number is worse than a complex honest one. He proposed a “depth and breadth” dashboard that would report three separate figures: the percentage of students who attend at least one session, the percentage who attend ten or more sessions, and the average number of sessions per attendee. “Then the public can see the full picture,” he said. “If participation is broad but shallow, that will be visible.” The dashboard, he added, would not require expensive new data collection, because the board already recorded session attendance for each student.

D
Not everyone was convinced. Another board member, Thomas Bell, worried that multiple measures would confuse parents. He suggested that the board keep the participation rate as a headline figure and publish the other numbers in an appendix. Ruiz responded that an appendix is where good information goes to die. “If the headline says 68 percent and the appendix says most students come once, people will remember the headline,” she said. “The format itself shapes what people believe.” The discussion became tense, but it also became more precise. The group agreed to test both approaches with a small group of parents before making a final decision, rather than relying on assumptions about how readers would respond.

E
In the following weeks, the researchers ran two parent evenings. At the first, they presented only the participation rate. At the second, they presented the three-figure dashboard. Afterwards, parents were asked what they had learned. Those who saw only the single rate were more likely to say that the clubs were “doing well” and less likely to mention that attendance was shallow. Parents who saw the dashboard were more likely to describe both strengths and weaknesses. The difference was not huge, but it was consistent. Nair, who had defended the single rate, admitted that the dashboard changed how people understood the situation. “I still think simplicity matters,” she said, “but I was wrong to assume that one number is always the simplest honest choice.”

F
The board has not yet made a final decision, but a compromise is emerging. The participation rate will remain on the first page of the annual report, but it will be accompanied by a short sentence that states the average number of sessions per student. If the average falls below a certain level, the report will include a warning. Haddad calls this a “minimum honest context.” Ruiz is not fully satisfied, but she accepts that change in public institutions is often gradual. “The important thing is that we are no longer pretending that one number tells the whole story,” she said. “A metric is a tool, not a truth.” The board will review the policy again next year, and the researchers have promised to publish their full data set so that others can check their conclusions. This commitment to transparency is seen by many as a positive step, ensuring that the debate remains evidence-based and open to public scrutiny.

grammar.title: 因果关系、条件和对比：段落间的逻辑与指代
grammar.explanation: 在英语写作中，表达因果、条件和对比时，除了使用从句（because, if, although），还常用名词化结构和连接副词来连接段落。例如：because of + 名词短语表示原因；if + 条件句表示条件；while/whereas 表示对比。同时，段落之间要用指代词（this, these, such, it）保持连贯，指代前文提到的概念。注意：this 单独使用时通常指代前一句或前一段的整体内容，而 this + 名词则明确指代某个名词。
grammar.example: Although the participation rate was climbing, the number of students who attended ten or more sessions had fallen sharply.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: ______ the heavy rain, the outdoor science fair was cancelled.
questions.explanation: “the heavy rain”是名词短语，表示原因，用Because of。Although和Despite表示让步，However是副词不能直接接名词。
questions.evidence: Because of the heavy rain, the outdoor science fair was cancelled.

questions.evidence: If students attend every session, they will receive a certificate.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: The participation rate rose, ______ the average number of sessions fell.
questions.explanation: 前后两个分句形成对比：参与率上升，而平均课程数下降，用whereas表示对比。
questions.evidence: The participation rate rose, whereas the average number of sessions fell.

questions.evidence: The board ignored the teachers' concerns. As a result, parents lost trust in the report.

questions.explanation: This单独使用指代前一句的整体内容（公布数据这件事），作主语。
questions.evidence: The researchers published their data. This allowed other scientists to check the results.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: ______ the dashboard was more complex, parents understood the situation better.
questions.explanation: 前后是让步关系：尽管仪表盘更复杂，家长却理解得更好，用Although。
questions.evidence: Although the dashboard was more complex, parents understood the situation better.
