materials.title: The Participation Rate Puzzle
materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，非官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。请先听/读对话，理解大意；然后完成10道题（单选、填空、判断正误/未提及）。听力部分注意说话人之间的自然插话和纠正。语法部分先看中文讲解，再完成8道新句练习题。最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。所有答案均在原文中有依据。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Thanks for coming, everyone. This is the weekly research meeting for the campus learning project. We need to decide whether to keep using the participation rate as our main measure.

Ben: Right. The participation rate is the percentage of students who attend at least one session each week. Last term it was 72 percent. This term it is 81 percent. The number looks good.

Maya: But does it really show learning? I mean, a student can attend and still not learn much.

Ben: That's true. But it is easy to collect. We just count who comes.

Lena: Sorry to interrupt, but I think we are missing something. Attendance is not the same as engagement. A student might sit in the room and do nothing.

Maya: Exactly. So if we want to measure learning, we need a different metric.

Ben: Wait, I didn't say the participation rate is useless. I said it is easy to collect. Those are different things.

Lena: You're right. Sorry. Let me rephrase. The participation rate is easy to collect, but it may not measure learning.

Maya: Good. So what else can we use? We have the end-of-term test scores.

Ben: Yes, but those come only once a term. They don't show weekly progress.

Lena: What about the short quizzes we give every two weeks? They are quick, and they show what students can do.

Maya: That's a good idea. But if we use quiz scores, we need to make sure the quizzes are fair. Otherwise the metric will be unfair too.

Ben: And if we change the metric, we have to explain it to the teachers. They will ask why.

Lena: We can explain that participation is an input measure, while quiz scores are an outcome measure. Inputs are what we do; outcomes are what students learn.

Maya: I like that distinction. So the participation rate tells us how many students come, but it does not tell us how much they learn.

Ben: OK, but I still think attendance matters. If students don't come, they can't learn.

Lena: True. So maybe we should keep both. Use participation to check access, and use quizzes to check learning.

Maya: That sounds balanced. But we need to be careful. If we report both, people may focus only on the participation rate because it is higher.

Ben: That's a real risk. The participation rate is 81 percent, but the average quiz score is only 64 percent. If we report both, the gap is clear.

Lena: And if we report only participation, the gap is hidden. That's why the metric matters.

Maya: So our recommendation is to report both, but to explain that they measure different things. Participation measures access; quizzes measure learning.

Ben: I agree. But we should also check whether the quizzes are reliable. If the quizzes are too easy, the scores will be high and the metric will mislead us.

Lena: Good point. We can ask two teachers to review the quizzes before we use them.

Maya: OK. So the plan is: keep the participation rate as an access measure, add quiz scores as a learning measure, and review the quizzes for fairness. Any objections?

Ben: None from me.

Lena: None. But can we also look at the dropout rate? If students leave, that is important too.

Maya: Yes, good idea. We can add the dropout rate as a third measure. But let's not make the report too complex.

Maya: Perfect. I'll write the draft and send it to you both by Friday. Thanks, everyone.

materials.title: The Ethics of Collecting and Using Information: A Community Data Project
materials.instructions: 项目原创模拟场景与数据，不是官方试卷。阅读文章后独立回答10题，再检查逐题依据。题目包含信息定位、论证范围、比较及推断；遇到词汇可用划词帮助，但使用帮助不算独立测评。语法先看规则，再做新语境练习。
materials.passage:
When a local library in the town of Riverton announced a project to collect residents' stories about the old market square, many people were excited. The project leader, Maya Chen, explained that the library wanted to create a digital archive of photos, interviews, and written memories. She said, "We are not just collecting facts; we are preserving the feelings and voices of the community." This statement captured the project's aim: to keep not only dates and events but also the emotions and personal perspectives that made the square meaningful to local people. Preserving such memories helps communities understand their shared identity and pass on local history to future generations. However, some residents worried about privacy. An elderly man named Mr. Patel asked, "Who will see my personal stories? Will my name be shared with everyone?" His concern was reasonable, as personal memories can reveal sensitive details about individuals and their families. Maya promised that all participants could choose whether to remain anonymous. She also said that the library would store the data securely and would not sell it to companies. This promise helped many people feel safer about joining the project, and more residents began to sign up for interviews.

As the project continued, a group of volunteers began to interview people in the square. One volunteer, a university student named Leo, recorded a conversation with a shop owner, Mrs. Garcia. She talked about how the market had changed over thirty years, describing the shops that had come and gone and the way the square had served as a meeting place for generations. Leo later wrote a short report for the library newsletter. In the report, he included a direct quote from Mrs. Garcia: "The square was like a big family room where everyone knew each other." However, Leo did not ask Mrs. Garcia if he could use her exact words in the newsletter. When Mrs. Garcia read the newsletter, she felt uncomfortable. She said, "I didn't know my words would be published for everyone to read. I thought the interview was just for the archive." This incident started a serious discussion about consent and the difference between collecting information for an archive and using it in public materials. The volunteers realized that agreeing to an interview did not automatically mean agreeing to public publication. They also learned that trust can be damaged when people feel their words have been used without their knowledge. This was a valuable lesson: even well-intentioned actions can harm if they ignore individual rights and expectations.

Maya called a meeting to address the problem. She invited volunteers, residents, and a local ethics teacher, Dr. Singh, to talk about the rules. Dr. Singh explained that when people share personal stories, they need to know exactly how their information will be used. She said, "Consent is not a single yes or no. It is a continuing conversation. You must ask again if the purpose changes." The group decided to create a clear consent form. The form would list every possible use of the information: archive only, newsletter, social media, or public presentation. Participants could tick the boxes they agreed to. They could also change their minds later. This gave people more control over their own stories and made the rules transparent. Maya apologized to Mrs. Garcia and removed her quote from the online version of the newsletter. Mrs. Garcia accepted the apology and agreed to stay in the project with a new consent form. The meeting showed that admitting mistakes and listening to concerns can strengthen a community project. It also demonstrated that ethical practices require ongoing attention and flexibility.

After the meeting, the project team made more changes. They trained volunteers to explain the consent form before every interview. They also added a step: before using any quote in a public material, the team must contact the person and read the quote to them. If the person says no, the team cannot use it. Leo said, "I learned that collecting information is not just about recording. It is about respecting the person who shared it." The library also started a monthly open meeting where residents could ask questions about the project. At the final community event, many people said they felt more confident about sharing their stories because they understood the rules. The project became a model for other towns. Maya concluded, "Trust is built slowly, but it can be lost quickly. Our job is to protect that trust every day."

A later review identified a limit to the promise of withdrawal. Deleting a quotation from the library website could not retrieve printed newsletters already taken home, nor could the team control screenshots made by readers. The revised form explained these limits before participation instead of promising total erasure. It also separated permission to use a named quotation from permission to publish an anonymous summary. Removing a name did not automatically remove every identifying detail: a distinctive job or a particular family event might still reveal the speaker. The team therefore checked proposed summaries with their contributors. This was more work than collecting a single signature, but the additional effort addressed risks that a secure storage system alone could not solve.

questions.prompt: What did Maya promise about participants' names?
options: They could choose to remain anonymous.

answers: They could choose to remain anonymous.

grammar.title: 叙事顺序、定语从句与授权范围的限定
grammar.explanation: 叙事中的一般过去时推进已完成事件，过去完成时had +过去分词可突出更早发生的动作；叙事中引用仍成立的事实不强制每句都回到过去。定语从句含关系词及谓语，例如a form that lists separate uses；“a local ethics teacher, Dr. Singh”只是同位语，不是定语从句。which可修饰物或指代前面整个事实；whose表示所属。because后接从句，because of后接名词短语。限定词only、may与被动结构决定授权范围，不能把approved for the archive扩大成approved for every use。

materials.transcript:
Maya: Hi, Daniel. You look busy. What are you working on?
Daniel: I'm helping the Riverside Community Archive. We collect old photos and letters from local families. Then we put them online.
Maya: That sounds nice. But I have a question. Do you ask people before you put their family photos online?
Daniel: Yes, we do. We always ask for written permission. Last month, a woman named Mrs. Chen gave us a box of letters. She signed a form, and she chose which letters we could share.
Maya: Good. But what about people in the photos? Maybe they didn't agree.
Daniel: That's a real problem. We learned that lesson last year. We uploaded a photo of a school class from 1965. One man in the photo called us. He was angry because he didn't want his childhood picture on the internet. We took the photo down the same day.
Maya: So what is your rule now?
Daniel: Now we have three rules. First, we ask the person who owns the item. Second, if the photo shows living people, we try to contact them. Third, if someone says no, we don't share it. We keep it in the archive building, but not online.
Maya: That sounds fair. But contacting everyone sounds hard.
Daniel: It is hard. Sometimes we can't find people. Then we don't publish the photo. We only publish photos of people who have agreed, or photos where everyone in the picture is no longer living.
Maya: Wait, is that last rule okay? Some families might still care.
Daniel: You're right. We changed that rule too. Now, even for old photos, we ask the family if we can find them. If we can't find the family, we wait.
Maya: I see. What about information like addresses or phone numbers in old letters?
Daniel: We remove private details. For example, last week I read a letter from 1972. It had a home address and a phone number. I blacked them out before we put the letter online. The letter is still useful for history, but the private information is hidden.
Maya: That's a good example. Do you also collect information from social media?
Daniel: No, we don't. We only use things that people give us directly. We don't copy posts from Facebook or WeChat. That would be wrong because people didn't give us permission.
Maya: What if a person gives you information, but later they change their mind?
Daniel: Then we remove it. Last spring, a man named Mr. Patel shared a recording of his father's stories. Two months later, he asked us to delete it. We deleted it immediately. We didn't argue.
Maya: That's respectful. How do you explain your rules to the public?
Daniel: We have a short page on our website. It says: 'We ask first. We protect private details. We remove things when people ask.' We also give talks at the library. Next month, I'm giving a talk about why consent matters.
Maya: I'd like to come. Can I bring my students?
Daniel: Of course. The talk is on Saturday at 2 p.m. It's free. But please tell me how many students are coming, because the room is small.
Maya: I will. Thanks, Daniel. This conversation made me think about my own photos.
Daniel: Me too. Actually, after our talk last year, I deleted some old photos of my friends from my phone. I didn't ask them before I posted those pictures. I felt bad.
Maya: That's honest. So the rules are not just for the archive.
Daniel: Right. They are for everyone who collects and shares information.

materials.title: Privacy and Public Interest: A Panel Discussion
materials.instructions: 阅读下面的文章，回答10个问题。文章是一篇模拟的英语学习材料，场景为虚构的公开讨论会。请先通读全文，再做题。问题类型包括单选、填空和判断正误/未提及。填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有问题与选项均为英文，解释为中文。
materials.passage:
Last Friday, a public library in the town of Riverton hosted a panel discussion titled “Privacy and Public Interest: Where Do We Draw the Line?” The event was part of a series of community talks on technology and society. Three speakers were invited: Dr. Maya Chen, a professor of information law; Mr. Daniel Okafor, a journalist who investigates data misuse; and Ms. Priya Nair, a software engineer who designs privacy tools. About eighty people attended, including students, local business owners, and retired residents. The panel aimed to explore how personal data collection and use can be balanced with the public good, a question that grows more urgent as technology becomes more embedded in daily life.

The moderator, Ms. Laura Simmons, opened the discussion by asking a simple question: “When a company collects personal data, how do we decide whether using that data serves the public good?” Dr. Chen began by explaining that privacy is not just about keeping secrets. She said, “Privacy is about control. When people know who has their information and why, they can make better choices.” She gave an example from her research: a hospital that shared patient records with a research team without telling patients. The research led to a useful discovery, but patients felt betrayed. “The problem was not the research itself,” Dr. Chen argued, “but the lack of transparency.” She emphasized that even well-intentioned projects can damage trust if people are not informed about how their data is used. Transparency, she noted, allows individuals to consent meaningfully and holds organizations accountable. Without it, she added, people cannot exercise real control over their personal information, and public trust in institutions may erode over time.

Mr. Okafor then described a case he had reported on. A delivery company had tracked its drivers’ locations even when they were off duty. The company claimed the data helped improve delivery times. However, Okafor found that managers also used the data to monitor workers’ private activities. “Public interest was the excuse,” he said, “but the real purpose was control.” He added that when journalists expose such practices, they often face legal pressure. “We need stronger laws to protect whistleblowers,” he concluded. Okafor explained that without legal protection, people who reveal wrongdoing inside organizations risk losing their jobs or facing lawsuits, which discourages others from speaking up. He argued that whistleblower protections are essential for a free press and for keeping powerful institutions in check. He also noted that such protections benefit society as a whole, because they ensure that important information about harmful practices reaches the public.

Ms. Nair offered a different perspective. She agreed that transparency matters, but she warned against making privacy rules too strict. “If we block all data sharing, we lose important benefits,” she said. For instance, her team had built an app that helps people with diabetes share their glucose levels with their doctors. Without data sharing, the app would not work. “The key is informed consent,” Nair explained. “Users must understand what they are sharing and with whom. Then they can decide.” She added that good design can make consent easier: clear menus, simple explanations, and the ability to withdraw permission at any time. She also noted that strict rules could prevent small companies from innovating, while large firms might find ways around them. Therefore, she argued, regulations should be flexible enough to support innovation while still protecting users.

During the question-and-answer session, a student asked whether public-interest projects should be allowed to use data without consent if the project is clearly beneficial. Dr. Chen replied that “beneficial” is hard to define. She suggested that an independent review board should evaluate each case. Such a board, she said, could include experts in law, ethics, and technology, as well as ordinary citizens, to ensure that decisions are not made solely by companies or governments. Okafor added that companies often label their projects as public interest to avoid criticism. He warned that without independent oversight, the label “public interest” can become a marketing tool rather than a genuine commitment. Nair proposed a middle path: “We can require companies to explain their data use in plain language. If they cannot explain it simply, they probably should not do it.” She also suggested that companies could publish regular reports on how data is used and who has access to it. Such reports, she noted, would allow the public to monitor practices and would encourage companies to act responsibly.

After the panel, many attendees said they had changed their minds. One retired teacher said, “I used to think privacy was only for people with something to hide. Now I see it affects everyone.” Another attendee, a local business owner, remarked that the discussion made him reconsider how his own company handles customer information. The library plans to host a follow-up session next month on how to protect personal data online. The panel did not reach a single conclusion, but it encouraged the audience to ask better questions. As Ms. Simmons noted in her closing remarks, the conversation is just beginning, and community involvement will be crucial in shaping fair and effective privacy rules.

materials.transcript:
Host: Good evening. Tonight we ask a simple but difficult question: when does the public's right to know beat a person's right to privacy? Our panel has three guests. Dr. Lin, a media lawyer. Mr. Carter, a former newspaper editor. And Ms. Okafor, a data-protection adviser. Dr. Lin, you wrote a report last year. What did you find?

Dr. Lin: We looked at forty court cases. In most of them, the judge said the public interest was strong because the story showed a real risk to safety. But in twelve cases, the judge said the privacy claim was stronger. The reason was simple: the information was only embarrassing, not dangerous.

Host: Mr. Carter, you edited a paper for twenty years. Did you ever publish a story that you later regretted?

Mr. Carter: Yes, once. We ran a story about a teacher who had a second job. The story was true, but it was not important. The teacher lost her job, and I still feel bad about it. That was a mistake. We should have asked: who does this help?

Ms. Okafor: I agree with that question. But I want to add a warning. A story that seems small can become big online. Last month, a hospital shared a patient's name by accident. The name was in a file that a journalist received. The journalist did not publish it, and that was the right choice. The public did not need the name. The public needed the safety report.

Host: Dr. Lin, is there a clear rule?

Dr. Lin: There is no single rule. But courts often ask three things. First, is the person powerful or public? Second, is the fact private or already known? Third, will publishing stop harm or cause harm? If the answer to the last question is 'cause harm', the privacy claim usually wins.

Mr. Carter: I would add a fourth question: can we tell the story without the private detail? Often we can. When I was an editor, we sometimes changed a name or a street. The story still worked. Readers understood the point.

Ms. Okafor: That is a good practice. But I want to be fair to journalists. Some stories are important because of a name. If a mayor uses public money for a private trip, the name matters. The public interest is strong there. The difference is that the mayor is responsible for public money.

Host: So the line is responsibility?

Ms. Okafor: Partly. Responsibility, power, and harm. If a person has power and the fact shows harm, publish. If the person has no power and the fact only embarrasses, do not publish.

Dr. Lin: I would say 'usually do not publish'. There can be exceptions. But the burden should be on the publisher to explain why the private detail is necessary.

Mr. Carter: And that explanation should be public. When we published the teacher story, we did not explain why. We just said it was true. True is not enough.

Host: One last question. What should a young journalist do tomorrow?

Ms. Okafor: Ask three questions before you publish. Who is hurt? Who is helped? Is the private detail necessary? Write the answers down. If you cannot write them, do not publish.

Mr. Carter: And talk to your editor early. Do not wait until the story is finished.

Dr. Lin: And keep a record. A record protects you and the person in the story.

Host: Thank you all. That is a useful place to stop.

grammar.title: 叙事时态、描述从句、原因与例子
grammar.explanation: 本课重点是把过去发生的事讲清楚，并用从句补充信息。第一，叙事时态：讲过去的事用一般过去时（we looked, I edited, she lost），讲更早的事可用过去完成时（had shared）。第二，描述从句：用 who/that/which 给名词加信息，如 a teacher who had a second job。第三，原因与例子：用 because / the reason was / for example 引出原因或例子，让观点有支撑。注意减少基础错误：主语和动词要一致（the public needs），可数名词单数前要有限定词（a story, the name），不要漏掉 be 动词（the story was true）。

materials.title: Shared Problems, Different Responses: A Simulated Community Case Study
materials.instructions: 项目原创模拟场景与数据，不是官方试卷。阅读文章后独立回答10题，再检查逐题依据。题目包含信息定位、论证范围、比较及推断；遇到词汇可用划词帮助，但使用帮助不算独立测评。语法先看规则，再做新语境练习。
materials.passage:
In the small coastal town of Marlow Bay, a problem that began far away gradually became impossible to ignore. For years, residents had noticed that the tide seemed to bring more plastic than fish. The town council, led by Mayor Elena Ruiz, first responded by organizing monthly beach clean-ups. These were popular, but they did not address the source of the waste. Meanwhile, a group of local fishermen, including Tomás Herrera, reported that their nets were catching fewer fish and more debris. They argued that the problem was not just local; it was regional, because currents carried rubbish from neighboring countries. The council, however, was reluctant to spend money on a problem that seemed to come from elsewhere.

A turning point came when a university research team published a study showing that microplastics had entered the local food chain. The study, led by Dr. Aisha Patel, was not without limitations: it relied on a small sample and had not yet been peer-reviewed. Nevertheless, it prompted the council to act. Mayor Ruiz proposed a pilot project to install floating barriers at the mouth of the bay. The barriers, designed by a local engineering firm, were intended to collect debris before it reached the beaches. Some council members objected, arguing that the barriers would interfere with fishing and might even harm marine life. After a heated debate, the council approved a six-month trial, with funding from a regional environmental grant.

The trial produced mixed results. The barriers did capture a significant amount of plastic, but they also trapped seaweed and small fish. Fishermen complained that the barriers made navigation difficult. Tomás Herrera, who had initially supported the project, now expressed doubts. "We need a solution that works for everyone," he said. "If we only focus on the barriers, we might ignore the root cause." The council decided to modify the design, adding escape hatches for marine life and reflective markers for boats. These changes reduced the bycatch, but the barriers still required frequent maintenance.

At the same time, a grassroots group called Blue Marlow began a campaign to reduce single-use plastics in local businesses. The group, founded by a retired teacher, Clara Nguyen, organized workshops and persuaded several restaurants to switch to biodegradable containers. This effort was smaller in scale than the barrier project, but it had a direct impact on daily habits. Some residents argued that the campaign was too focused on individual responsibility, while corporations continued to produce most of the waste. Clara responded that local action could inspire broader change. "If we wait for global agreements," she said, "we may never start."

The town's experience attracted attention from a regional network of coastal communities. Representatives from three neighboring towns visited Marlow Bay to learn about both the barriers and the plastic-reduction campaign. They noted that Marlow Bay's approach combined technological and social measures, which was unusual. However, they also observed that the town had advantages: a relatively wealthy population, a supportive mayor, and access to grant funding. These conditions might not exist elsewhere. As a result, the visitors concluded that while the barrier project could be adapted, the plastic-reduction campaign might be more transferable, because it required fewer resources.

Back in Marlow Bay, the council commissioned a second study to evaluate the long-term effects of the barriers. This study, conducted by an independent consultancy, found that the barriers had reduced plastic on beaches by about 30 percent, but at a cost of $50,000 per year in maintenance. The report recommended a combination of barriers and upstream measures, such as working with manufacturers to reduce packaging. It also noted that public support was crucial: without community buy-in, even well-designed projects could fail.

The consultants also cautioned against reading the beach figure as a measurement of total marine pollution. Their survey counted visible items on selected beaches; it did not measure all particles in the water or establish what happened farther along the coast. Storms and changes in collection schedules could influence the counts. A neighbouring town was proposed as a comparison site, but it differed in tourist numbers and tidal conditions, so a simple comparison would need careful qualification. The council agreed to report those differences, together with maintenance costs and unintended effects. A policy could be useful without being sufficient, and a positive local result was not a guarantee that another town would obtain the same benefit.

Mayor Ruiz reflected on the lessons. "We started with a local problem, but we learned that it was connected to global patterns," she said. "The barriers were not a silver bullet, but they taught us how to experiment and adapt. The plastic campaign showed us that small actions can add up. In the end, the most important thing was to keep the conversation going." The town now plans to share its findings with the regional network, hoping that other communities can learn from both its successes and its mistakes.

One resident, a shop owner named Mr. Chen, summarized the mood: "We are not heroes. We just tried something, and when it didn't work perfectly, we changed it. That is what a community does."

grammar.explanation: 比较要说明比较的对象和维度，如smaller in scale than。while既可表示同时发生，也可表达对比，判断要看两边信息；不能把它一律解释成“虽然”。although +从句与despite +名词/-ing都可表示让步。可能性可用may/might，但不能当成已证实因果。第二条件句可表达与当前事实相反或较不可能的情况，if +过去式，主句would/could +原形；过去反事实则用had +过去分词及would have +过去分词。统计范围限定和程度词要准确，部分有效不等于完全解决。

materials.title: Shared Problems, Local Solutions: A Community Garden Meeting
materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，非官方雅思试题，也不代表任何官方分数。请先听/读英文材料，再完成10道题（听力与阅读混合）。听力部分注意不同说话人的自然轮换与自我更正。语法部分先用中文讲解新规则，再完成8道新句练习题。口语与写作任务请用英文完成。所有答案依据材料原文，NOT GIVEN 题请参考中文解释中“缺失事实”的说明。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Okay, everyone, thanks for coming. This is the first meeting of the Riverside Community Garden group. We have twelve people here tonight. Let me start with the problem. Last summer, the empty lot on Mill Street was full of rubbish. People dumped old chairs and broken TVs there. It smelled bad, and children could not play outside.

Daniel: Sorry, can I say something? I live on Mill Street. The rubbish was bad, yes, but the bigger problem was the rats. We saw rats every evening. My neighbour called the city three times.

Maya: Right, thank you, Daniel. So the shared problem is rubbish and rats. Now, what can we do locally? I have three ideas. First, we ask the city for two large bins. Second, we start a garden club and grow vegetables. Third, we put up a sign that says “Please keep this place clean.”

Priya: I like the garden idea, but I have a question. Who will water the plants in summer? Most of us work during the day.

Maya: Good point. We could make a watering rota. Each person waters once a week. If we have twelve members, that is only twelve weeks of watering.

Daniel: Wait, twelve members and one week each — that is twelve weeks, but summer is only about ten weeks. So we need two more weeks. Maybe families can share.

Maya: You are right. Let me correct that. We need a rota of about ten weeks, and some people can water twice.

Priya: Also, the city bins are not free. I checked online. Two large bins cost 80 dollars each year. That is 160 dollars. We do not have that money now.

Daniel: But we could raise money. Last year the school raised 300 dollars with a cake sale. If we sell cakes and old books, we might get 200 dollars.

Maya: That is a good estimate. So, condition: if we raise 200 dollars, we can pay for the bins and still have 40 dollars for seeds.

Priya: Although the cake sale is a good idea, it takes a lot of time. I work on Saturdays. Could we do it on a Sunday?

Maya: Yes, Sunday is better. Let us agree: the cake sale is on Sunday, the 14th of next month. Daniel, can you ask the school for the tables?

Daniel: Sure. I will ask them tomorrow. But I should say — I am not sure the school will say yes. They are often busy.

Maya: That is fine. Even if they say no, we can use my garage. It is small, but it works.

Priya: One more thing. The sign. Who will make it? I can paint, but I am not very good at writing English.

Maya: I can write the words, and you can paint the letters. That is a good team. So, to summarise: we ask the city for bins, we plan a Sunday cake sale, we make a watering rota, and we put up a sign. Any other ideas?

Daniel: What about the rats? Bins help, but we also need to cut the long grass near the wall. Rats hide in tall grass.

Maya: Excellent point. So we add one more job: cut the grass. We can do that next Saturday morning. I will bring tools. Priya, can you bring gloves?

Priya: Yes, I have four pairs. I will bring them.

Maya: Great. So our next meeting is in two weeks. Thank you, everyone. This was a very useful discussion.

materials.title: Incentives in the Lecture Hall: A Simulated Academic Listening and Grammar Lesson
materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟教学材料，非官方雅思试题，也不代表任何官方分数。请先通读文章，理解短期与长期激励的对比；然后完成10道阅读理解题（题型包括单选、填空、标题匹配和True/False/Not Given）。之后学习语法部分（概括、比较、推测、条件与让步），并完成8道独立语法题。最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。所有题目答案均可在文中找到依据，填空题答案必须与原文完全一致。
materials.passage:
In a crowded lecture hall last Tuesday, Dr. Elena Marsh began her talk with a simple question: “Why do we often choose a small reward now over a larger one later?” The audience, mostly second-year university students, shifted in their seats. Dr. Marsh, a behavioral economist, was not asking for a moral judgment. She was introducing a framework for understanding how incentives shape decisions over time. Her aim was practical: to show how the timing of rewards and punishments influences the choices people make, often without realizing it.

A. Short-term incentives are rewards or punishments that occur soon after a behavior. They are powerful because they feel immediate. For example, a student might study for an hour to avoid failing a quiz the next day. The quiz is a short-term incentive: it is close, concrete, and easy to imagine. Dr. Marsh noted that short-term incentives often work well for simple tasks, such as completing a weekly assignment or attending a review session. Because the consequence arrives quickly, the connection between effort and outcome is clear, which makes action easier to start. However, they can also encourage narrow thinking. If a student only studies to pass tomorrow’s quiz, they may ignore deeper understanding. In other words, short-term incentives are effective at driving behavior, but they do not automatically produce good learning.

B. Long-term incentives, by contrast, are rewards or punishments that arrive much later. They require what Dr. Marsh called “mental time travel”: imagining a future self who benefits from today’s effort. A student who studies consistently for a semester to earn a scholarship is responding to a long-term incentive. Such incentives are harder to sustain because the reward is distant and uncertain. The future self can feel abstract, and the payoff may seem easy to postpone. Yet they often lead to more durable learning and better career outcomes, since they encourage steady effort rather than last-minute cramming. Dr. Marsh pointed out that long-term incentives depend on trust—trust that the future reward will actually arrive. Without that trust, the distant goal loses much of its motivating power.

C. The lecture then turned to a common mistake: people often overestimate their future self-control. Dr. Marsh described a study (simulated for this lecture) in which students promised to exercise more in the coming month. Most believed they would succeed. In reality, only a small fraction kept their promise. This gap between intention and action is called the “intention–behavior gap.” Dr. Marsh argued that this gap is not a sign of laziness but a predictable feature of human psychology. People genuinely intend to act, yet their plans often fail when the moment of effort arrives. She suggested that combining short-term and long-term incentives can help. For instance, a student might set a small weekly reward (like a movie night) for completing study goals, while keeping the long-term scholarship in mind. In this way, the immediate reward provides momentum, and the distant goal provides direction.

D. During the question period, a student named Marcus asked, “If short-term incentives are so powerful, why don’t we just use them all the time?” Dr. Marsh replied, “That’s a fair question. Short-term incentives can be effective, but they may crowd out intrinsic motivation—the desire to learn for its own sake. If you reward a student for reading with a small payment, they might start reading only for the payment. So, while short-term incentives have their place, they should be used carefully.” Another student, Priya, asked about deadlines. Dr. Marsh explained that deadlines are a type of short-term incentive, but they can also create anxiety. She recommended breaking large tasks into smaller deadlines to balance urgency and stress. This approach keeps the motivating pressure of a deadline while reducing the risk of feeling overwhelmed.

E. Toward the end of the lecture, Dr. Marsh summarized her main point: “Neither short-term nor long-term incentives are inherently good or bad. The key is to design them so that they support each other. If you can make the short-term rewarding and the long-term meaningful, you are more likely to persist.” She then gave a final example: a language learner who practices ten minutes every day (short-term habit) to prepare for a fluency exam next year (long-term goal). The daily practice is small, but it builds momentum. The exam is distant, but it gives direction. Together, the two kinds of incentive form a system rather than a choice between opposites.

F. As the students left the hall, many were discussing how they might apply these ideas to their own study habits. One student remarked, “I never thought about how my daily choices connect to my future self.” Another said, “Maybe I should set a small reward for finishing my weekly reading.” Dr. Marsh’s lecture had done more than define terms; it had invited the audience to reconsider the incentives in their own lives.

materials.title: Short-Term Sparks and Long-Term Fires: A Lecture on Incentives
materials.instructions: 本材料为模拟教学练习，不是官方雅思试题，也不代表任何官方分数。请先听/读英文讲座稿，完成10道听力理解题（单选、填空、判断正误/未提及）。然后学习语法规则（概括、比较、推测、条件与让步），完成8道新句语法题。最后进行口语与写作迁移练习。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。
materials.transcript:
Good morning, everyone. Today I want to contrast two kinds of incentives: short-term rewards and long-term commitments. Let me start with a simple example. Imagine a company offers a bonus for each sale made this month. That is a short-term incentive. It produces quick action. But it may also produce rushed work and unhappy customers. Now imagine the same company offers a yearly profit share. That is a long-term incentive. It encourages careful decisions and patient relationship building. Neither is automatically better. The right choice depends on the task and the people.

Let me give you a second example from education. A student who receives a small prize for finishing homework tonight may study for an hour. A student who receives a scholarship after two years of steady effort may study for many months. The first reward is immediate; the second is delayed. Immediate rewards are powerful, but they fade quickly. Delayed rewards are weaker at first, but they can shape habits.

Now, a common mistake is to assume that short-term incentives always harm long-term goals. That is not true. If the short-term reward is designed well, it can support the long-term goal. For example, a weekly team check-in can be a short-term routine that strengthens a long-term project. The key is alignment. When the short-term action moves you toward the long-term aim, the two work together. When it pulls you away, they conflict.

Another point: people often underestimate how much context matters. In a fast-changing market, short-term incentives may be necessary because long-term plans become outdated. In a stable environment, long-term incentives may be more effective because they reward consistency. So we should not ask, “Which incentive is best?” We should ask, “Which incentive fits this situation?”

Let me add a caution about measurement. If you measure only short-term output, people may ignore long-term quality. If you measure only long-term results, people may lose motivation during the long wait. A balanced system uses both. For instance, a sales team might receive a monthly bonus for customer satisfaction and a yearly bonus for repeat business. The monthly bonus is short-term; the yearly bonus is long-term. Together they cover both speed and trust.

What about unintended effects? Suppose a manager promises a reward for every complaint resolved within one day. Employees may close cases quickly without solving the real problem. The short-term incentive works, but the long-term outcome gets worse. This is why designers must predict how people will respond. If the reward is too narrow, people will optimize the narrow measure. If the reward is broad, people may not know what to do. The design challenge is to be specific enough to guide action, but broad enough to avoid gaming.

Finally, consider fairness. Even a well-designed incentive can fail if people believe it is unfair. If one team receives a large bonus and another team receives nothing for similar work, trust may drop. Trust is a long-term asset. Short-term savings from unequal rewards can cost long-term cooperation. Therefore, communicate the rules clearly and apply them consistently.

To summarize: short-term incentives create energy; long-term incentives create direction. Good systems use short-term rewards to start motion and long-term rewards to sustain it. The best design aligns the two, measures both, predicts responses, and protects fairness. Thank you. I’ll take questions now.

materials.title: Learning from Failure: A Simulated Case Study of an Adult Education Centre
materials.instructions: 阅读下面的文章，回答10个问题。文章是关于一个成人教育中心如何从失败中学习的模拟案例。请先通读全文，再做题。题目类型包括单选、填空、匹配和判断正误/未提及。填空答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。
materials.passage:
A. In 2022, the Westbridge Adult Education Centre launched a new evening course called 'Digital Skills for Work'. The centre expected 40 students, but only 12 enrolled. The course ran for eight weeks, and by the end, only five students were still attending. This was a serious problem, because low enrolment and poor attendance meant the course was not achieving its purpose of helping adults improve their digital skills for employment. The centre's director, Maria Chen, was disappointed. She called a meeting with the course teacher, David Kim, and the administrator, Sarah Patel. They wanted to understand why the course had failed, rather than simply accepting the poor result. This decision to investigate rather than ignore the problem was the first step towards improvement.

B. At the meeting, David said, 'The main problem was the time. Many students told me they finished work at 6 p.m. and could not get to the centre by 6:30. The course started too early.' This comment pointed to a practical scheduling issue: students needed enough time to travel from their workplaces to the centre. Sarah added, 'We also advertised the course only on our website. Most of our students don't check the website often. They use social media.' Her point suggested that the centre had used the wrong communication channel to reach its audience. Maria listened and took notes. She said, 'So we need a later start time and better advertising. But let's not guess. Let's collect evidence.' Her response showed the importance of testing assumptions rather than acting on opinion alone, and it set the direction for the team's next steps.

C. The team decided to gather data. They sent a short survey to all 12 students who enrolled. Seven students replied, which gave the team a reasonable amount of feedback to work with. The survey asked: Why did you leave? What time would suit you better? How did you hear about the course? The answers showed that five students left because of the time, and two left because they found the course too difficult. This revealed two separate problems: scheduling and the level of difficulty. The survey also showed that most students heard about the course from a friend, not from the website. This supported Sarah's earlier point about advertising and confirmed that word of mouth was a powerful channel the centre had not been using.

D. Maria also looked at the enrolment numbers for other courses. She noticed that courses starting at 7 p.m. had higher attendance than those starting at 6:30. She shared this with the team. 'This is useful evidence,' she said. 'It suggests that a later start time could help. But we need to test it.' By comparing different courses, Maria was able to identify a pattern that supported the survey findings. However, she understood that evidence alone does not prove a solution will work; it must be tested in practice. This cautious approach prevented the team from making changes based on a single source of information.

E. The team made two changes for the next course. First, they moved the start time to 7 p.m. Second, they advertised on social media and asked current students to tell their friends. They also added a short 'taster' session before the course began, so students could try before enrolling. This gave potential students a chance to experience the course and decide whether it suited them. The new course started in January 2023. This time, 28 students enrolled, and 22 completed the course. The completion rate was much higher, which suggested that the changes had made a positive difference and that the evidence-based approach had been worthwhile.

F. However, not everything improved. The teacher, David, reported that some students still found the material too difficult. 'The taster session helped, but we need to check students' levels before they join,' he said. Maria agreed. 'We learned that collecting evidence is important, but we also need to act on it quickly. Next time, we will ask students about their level before the course starts.' This showed that improvement is an ongoing process, and that solving one problem can reveal another. The team accepted this as a natural part of learning rather than a new failure.

G. The centre now has a simple rule: after every course, they hold a short 'learning review'. They ask three questions: What worked? What didn't work? What will we change? They write down the answers and share them with all teachers. This routine helps the organisation turn experience into shared knowledge, so that lessons learned in one course benefit future courses and other teachers. Maria says, 'Failure is not the end. It is information. If we use it well, we can improve.'

H. This case shows how an organisation can learn from failure. It is not enough to feel bad about a bad result. You need to find out why it happened, collect evidence, make changes, and then check if the changes worked. The Westbridge Centre did this, and their courses are now more successful. Their experience demonstrates that failure can be valuable when it is treated as a source of information rather than simply as a setback, and that a systematic approach to learning from mistakes can turn a disappointing outcome into lasting improvement.

materials.transcript:
[Meeting room, Riverside Community Clinic. Present: Dr. Maya Chen (facilitator), Tom Baker (senior nurse), Priya Shah (quality lead), and Ben Okafor (junior administrator).]

Maya: Thanks for coming. Today we’re reviewing the medication-error incident from last month. The goal is to understand what happened and what we can change. Tom, can you start with the timeline?

Tom: Sure. On the 14th, a patient was given the wrong dose of a blood thinner. The nurse on duty was experienced, but the shift was short-staffed. The error was caught two hours later during a routine check.

Priya: Sorry to interrupt—was the patient harmed?

Tom: No, thankfully. The patient was monitored and was fine. But we need to learn from it.

Maya: Right. Ben, you looked at the incident report. What stood out?

Ben: The report was filed three days late. That’s a problem because details get forgotten. Also, the form asks for the nurse’s name, but not for the system factors—like workload or interruptions.

Priya: That’s a key point. If we only blame the individual, we miss the bigger picture. I’d suggest we revise the form to include a section on working conditions.

Maya: Good. Tom, what about the training?

Tom: The nurse had completed the online module, but it was six months old. The module doesn’t cover new drug names. So maybe we need shorter, more frequent updates.

Ben: I agree. And we could add a quick team huddle before each shift to review high-risk medications.

Maya: Let’s note that. Priya, you mentioned earlier that other clinics have tried a “no-blame” reporting system. Can you explain?

Priya: Yes. In a no-blame system, staff report errors without fear of punishment. The focus is on learning, not on blaming. But it only works if leadership supports it and if reports are acted on quickly.

Maya: So we need both a culture change and a process change. Tom, how did staff react to the incident?

Tom: Some were anxious. A few worried they’d be punished. But after the manager explained the no-blame approach, people became more open. One nurse said she now feels safer reporting near-misses.

Maya: That’s encouraging. Ben, can you summarize the action points?

Ben: Sure. First, revise the incident form to include system factors. Second, introduce short monthly training updates. Third, pilot a pre-shift huddle for high-risk drugs. Fourth, communicate the no-blame policy clearly to all staff.

Maya: And who will lead each action?

Ben: I can lead the form revision with Priya. Tom can lead the training updates. And the huddle pilot—maybe Priya and I can co-lead.

Priya: That works for me. But we need a timeline. Can we aim to start the pilot next month?

Maya: Yes, let’s set a review meeting in six weeks to check progress. Any other comments?

Tom: Just one. We should also share the learning with the wider network. Other clinics might benefit.

Maya: Agreed. I’ll draft a short summary for the regional meeting. Thanks, everyone. Let’s make sure this becomes a learning opportunity, not just a report.

materials.title: The Evidence Integration Seminar
materials.instructions: 这是一份为B2–C1学习者设计的原创阅读材料，主题为跨学科证据整合研讨会。请先通读全文，注意段落A/B/C的标记。然后完成10道题目：单选题、填空题、匹配题（以单选形式呈现）和判断题（True/False/Not Given）。填空题答案必须与原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。本材料为模拟教育内容，并非官方雅思试题，也不代表任何真实考试分数。
materials.passage:
Dr. Lin Wei, a historian at a mid-sized university, had spent three years studying a set of letters written by merchants in a port city during the 1780s. The letters described shipments of tea, silk, and porcelain, and they mentioned frequent delays caused by storms. Lin believed the letters offered strong evidence that the port's economy had declined sharply in that decade. She had presented this conclusion at two local conferences, and her colleagues had generally accepted it. However, when she was invited to join a seminar on interdisciplinary evidence, she began to question whether her interpretation was complete. The invitation came at an opportune moment, since she had recently noticed gaps in her argument that she could not explain using historical sources alone. These gaps troubled her: the letters were vivid and detailed, but they represented only a handful of merchants, and she wondered whether their experiences reflected the wider reality of the port.

The seminar, held over two days in a modern conference room, brought together twelve researchers from history, economics, climate science, and archaeology. The organizer, Professor Marta Ruiz, opened the first session by explaining the goal: to examine how different fields define and evaluate evidence, and to see whether combining methods could lead to more reliable conclusions. She warned the group that each discipline has its own standards, and that mixing them without care could produce confusion rather than clarity. This warning set the tone for the discussions that followed, encouraging participants to explain their methods carefully rather than simply presenting their findings. Ruiz emphasized that interdisciplinary work requires translation: each expert must make their assumptions explicit so that others can assess them fairly.

On the first afternoon, Dr. Chen Hao, an economist, presented data on shipping insurance rates from the same port. His records showed that insurance premiums had actually fallen slightly between 1782 and 1788, which suggested that merchants and insurers considered the risk of loss to be decreasing, not increasing. Chen argued that if the economy had been declining sharply, insurance rates would likely have risen, because insurers would have demanded higher payments to cover greater uncertainty. Lin listened carefully and noted that her letters had focused on individual complaints, not on overall trends. She realized that her evidence was selective: the merchants who wrote the letters might have been unusually unlucky, or they might have exaggerated their difficulties to justify higher prices. Either way, their personal accounts could not by themselves represent the experience of the whole port. Chen added that insurance data, while more systematic, also had limits, since it covered only insured cargo and might miss smaller traders.

A climate scientist, Dr. Priya Nair, then shared reconstructions of regional weather patterns based on tree rings and ice cores. Her data indicated that the 1780s had indeed experienced several severe storms, but they were part of a longer period of unusual weather that had begun in the 1770s and continued into the 1790s. Nair cautioned that a few stormy years do not necessarily mean economic decline; societies often adapt by changing routes or building better ships. Her evidence supported the merchants' reports of storms but did not confirm that the port's economy had collapsed. In fact, she suggested that the merchants' letters might reflect short-term disruption rather than long-term failure, and that the distinction between the two was essential for a fair interpretation. She also noted that tree-ring data provide annual but not monthly resolution, so they cannot pinpoint specific storms mentioned in the letters.

On the second day, an archaeologist, Dr. Samuel Okafor, showed photographs of pottery and tools excavated from the port's harbor. The artifacts suggested that trade had continued throughout the 1780s, though the types of goods had changed. For example, there were fewer luxury items and more everyday utensils, which might indicate a shift in consumer demand rather than a total economic failure. Okafor also pointed out that the excavation had covered only a small area of the harbor, so the findings could not be generalized to the entire port. He emphasized that archaeological evidence is often fragmentary and must be interpreted alongside written records rather than in isolation. He suggested that the shift from luxury to everyday goods might reflect a broader change in taste or in trade networks, not simply a response to economic hardship.

By the end of the seminar, Lin had revised her conclusion. She now argued that the port's economy had experienced a period of adjustment, not a sharp decline. The letters were still valuable evidence of individual experiences, but they needed to be combined with insurance records, climate data, and archaeological findings to produce a more balanced picture. Professor Ruiz closed the seminar by reminding the participants that evidence is rarely complete, and that good research requires both confidence and humility. She added that interdisciplinary work is not about replacing one field's methods with another's, but about building a fuller understanding through careful comparison. The seminar had shown that each discipline offered a partial view, and that only by combining them could the researchers approach a more reliable account.

After the seminar, Lin returned to her office and wrote a short note to herself: "Ask not only what the evidence shows, but also what it leaves out." She planned to revise her conference paper and to include a section on the limitations of her original sources. She also decided to invite Chen, Nair, and Okafor to collaborate on a larger study of the port's economic history. The seminar had not given her a simple answer, but it had given her better questions.

materials.title: Seminar Evidence Integration: The Community Garden Study
materials.instructions: 这是一份模拟英语听力与阅读练习，不是官方雅思考试，也不代表任何分数。请先听录音（或阅读文本），然后完成10道题。题目类型包括单选、填空、匹配（以单选形式）和判断正误/未提及。填空答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。语法部分先学习新规则，再完成8道题。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。请仔细阅读每个问题，注意证据的准确性。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for coming to this cross-disciplinary seminar. Today we’re looking at the community garden project and how different departments collected evidence. Let’s start with you, Leo. You were in charge of the soil tests, right?
Leo: Yes, that’s right. We took soil samples from three areas: the north bed, the south bed, and the new east bed. The north and south beds had good pH levels, around 6.5. But the east bed was more acidic, about 5.8. We think that’s because of the pine trees nearby.
Maya: Interesting. So the east bed needs treatment before planting. Now, Priya, you looked at the water usage. What did you find?
Priya: Well, we measured water consumption over eight weeks. The drip irrigation system used about 30% less water than the sprinkler system. But we also noticed that the sprinkler system lost more water to evaporation, especially on hot days. So the drip system is more efficient.
Maya: Good. And what about the plant growth data, Sam?
Sam: I compared two types of tomatoes: cherry and beefsteak. The cherry tomatoes grew faster in the first month, but the beefsteak tomatoes produced more fruit by the end of the season. However, we had a problem with pests in the south bed, which affected the beefsteak plants. So the yield data might be lower than expected.
Maya: Thanks, Sam. That’s an important point about pests. Now, Chen, you interviewed the volunteers. What did they say about the project?
Chen: Most volunteers said they enjoyed working in the garden, but some mentioned that the tools were often missing or broken. Also, a few volunteers felt that the training session at the beginning was too short. They wanted more guidance on planting and watering.
Maya: So we have some operational issues to address. Let’s move on to the budget. Hana, you reviewed the finances. Can you summarize?
Hana: Sure. The total budget for the project was $5,000. We spent $2,000 on seeds and plants, $1,500 on tools and equipment, and $800 on water bills. The remaining $700 was used for unexpected repairs to the fence. So we stayed within budget, but there’s little left for next season.
Maya: Good to know. Now, let’s think about how to integrate these findings. Leo, you mentioned the soil pH. How does that relate to the plant growth data?
Leo: Well, the east bed’s low pH might explain why the plants there grew more slowly. But we didn’t plant tomatoes in the east bed this season, so we can’t directly compare. However, the north and south beds had similar pH, yet the south bed had pest problems, which affected yield. So soil pH alone doesn’t tell the whole story.
Maya: Exactly. And Priya, how does water usage connect to plant growth?
Priya: The drip system was used mainly in the north bed, and that bed had good growth. But the south bed also used drip irrigation and had pest issues. So water efficiency is important, but pests can override that benefit.
Maya: So we need to consider multiple factors together. Chen, did the volunteers’ feedback mention anything about pests or water?
Chen: Not directly. But some volunteers said they had trouble knowing when to water, which might relate to the training. And a few mentioned seeing insects on the plants but didn’t report them because they weren’t sure who to tell.
Maya: That’s a key gap in communication. Sam, any final thoughts from your side?
Sam: Yes, I think we should repeat the experiment next season with better pest control and maybe test different tomato varieties in the east bed after adjusting the soil. Also, we should document everything more carefully so we can compare across beds.
Maya: Great. So to sum up, we have evidence from soil, water, plant growth, volunteer feedback, and budget. Each piece adds something, but no single piece gives the full picture. Our next step is to design a more integrated study for next year. Thank you all.

materials.title: The Library Roof Decision
materials.instructions: 项目原创模拟场景与数据，不是官方试卷。阅读文章后独立回答10题，再检查逐题依据。题目包含信息定位、论证范围、比较及推断；遇到词汇可用划词帮助，但使用帮助不算独立测评。语法先看规则，再做新语境练习。
materials.passage:
A. The town of Marlow Vale faced a problem. Its public library, a small brick building on King Street, had a leaking roof. Rain had damaged books and computers. The town council had to decide whether to repair the roof or move the library to a larger building near the train station. The council had a budget of £120,000. The repair would cost about £80,000. Moving would cost £150,000, but the new building would be bigger and easier to reach. The council asked the town's residents for their opinions. Exactly 1,620 adults answered an online survey. Most of them said they wanted a bigger library. However, only 18 percent of the town's 9,000 adults completed the survey. The council knew that this was not a perfect picture of public opinion. The low response rate meant that the survey results might not represent the views of the whole community. For example, people who did not use the library or who were too busy might not have taken part. Therefore, the council decided to gather more information before making a final decision.

B. The council held two public meetings. At the first meeting, many older residents said they liked the current library because it was close to their homes. They did not want to walk to the station. They also said that the library was a familiar place where they felt comfortable. At the second meeting, younger residents and parents said the library was too small for children's activities. They wanted more space. One parent said, “We need a place where kids can read and play.” A local business owner offered to give £20,000 to help with the move. But he also said the council should wait for more information. The council's finance officer warned that repair costs might rise. She said, “The roof is old. We may find more problems when we start work.” She explained that old buildings often have hidden damage, such as weak walls or outdated wiring, which could increase the total cost. The council therefore needed to be careful with its limited budget.

C. The council decided to take a middle path. They voted to repair the roof first, using £80,000. They also agreed to spend £10,000 on a study about moving the library in the future. The study will look at costs, parking, and bus routes. It will also consider how many people use the library and what services they need. The council will receive the study results in six months. The remaining £30,000 will be kept for emergencies. The council leader explained, “We are not saying no to a new library. We are saying we need better evidence before we spend a large amount of money.” Some residents were unhappy. They said the council was too slow. Others were pleased. They said the council was careful with public money. The leader added that the council would consider all options once the study was complete.

D. The library will stay open during the roof repair. However, the children's reading room will be closed for three weeks. The council will put a temporary reading area in the town hall. The library staff will move 2,000 children's books to the town hall. The repair work will start on 15 March and finish by 30 April. The council has promised to hold another public meeting in May to discuss interim questions and the future of the library; the completed six-month study would not yet be available. The town's newspaper, the Marlow Vale Gazette, will report on the meeting. The council also said it would put all documents online so that residents can read them. This includes the survey results, the study report, and the cost estimates. The leader added, “We want people to see the facts. Then we can make a better decision together.” The council hopes that more residents will take part in the discussion this time. To encourage this, the council plans to advertise the meeting on its website and in local shops, and to provide a summary of the documents in plain language. The leader stressed that the emergency repair work would not affect the library's opening hours, except for the children's room. He also thanked the residents who had already shared their views and urged others to get involved.

E. The finance officer proposed comparing the options over ten years rather than judging them by their initial prices alone. Repairing the roof might be cheaper immediately but leave expensive maintenance later; relocation might have higher initial costs but lower running costs. Neither possibility had yet been quantified. The study would therefore present several scenarios instead of one apparently precise forecast. It would state assumptions about energy prices, building condition and expected use, and show how conclusions changed when those assumptions changed. The officer also warned against treating the possible business donation as money already available. A promise conditional on a move could not finance a decision to stay. Keeping an emergency reserve reduced the risk of abandoning essential work halfway through, although it left less money for other services. The council accepted that choosing a cautious sequence still had an opportunity cost: residents would wait longer for any extra space. Evidence could make that trade-off clearer, but could not remove the need to choose.

materials.title: Public Decisions with Incomplete Evidence: A Simulated Listening and Grammar Lesson
materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，不是官方雅思试题，也不代表任何官方分数。请先听录音（或阅读文字稿），完成10道听力题；然后学习语法讲解，完成8道语法题；最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。听力题和语法题均为英文题干，解释为中文。注意：听力文字稿中不会读出答案列表。
materials.transcript:
Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for coming. We need to decide today whether to approve the new community garden on the old parking lot. But first, I want to be clear: we don't have all the information yet. The soil test results won't be back until next week. So we're deciding with incomplete evidence. That's the reality.

Daniel: Sorry, Maya, can I just check something? You said the soil test results are not back. Does that mean we have no idea about contamination? Or do we have some early indication?

Maya: Good question. We have an early indication from a quick scan. It suggests low risk, but it's not a full test. So we should treat it as uncertain.

Priya: I think we should postpone the decision. If we approve now and the soil is bad, we'll have to close the garden and spend more money. That seems risky.

Daniel: I understand that, Priya. But if we wait, we lose the planting season. The grant money expires in June. So waiting has a cost too.

Maya: Exactly. So the question is: how do we make a good decision when we can't be sure? I suggest we approve a conditional plan. We say yes to the garden, but only if the full soil test is acceptable. If it's not, we stop. That way we don't lose the season, and we don't take a big risk.

Priya: Hmm. That sounds reasonable. But who pays for the full test? And what happens if the test is borderline—not clearly good, not clearly bad?

Maya: The city has agreed to pay for the full test. For borderline results, we ask an independent expert to review. That's in the draft plan.

Daniel: OK, I'm starting to agree. But I want to add one thing: we should tell the public exactly what we know and what we don't know. If we pretend we're certain, and then something goes wrong, people will lose trust.

Maya: Yes, transparency matters. So the plan includes a public note: 'We are approving this garden with conditions because the evidence is incomplete. We will publish the full test results when they arrive.'

Priya: I like that. But I'm still worried about the money. If the test fails, we've already spent money on design. Can we get that back?

Maya: No, design costs are sunk. We can't get them back. But they're small compared to the cost of a bad garden. So the conditional plan still makes sense.

Daniel: Wait—did you say the design costs are sunk? I thought the grant covered design. If the grant covered it, then it's not our money, right?

Maya: The grant covers design only if we start construction. If we cancel, we pay back the design money. So it's not fully sunk. Sorry, I misspoke. Let me correct that: design costs are recoverable only if we cancel before construction. So they're not completely sunk.

Priya: OK, that changes things a little. So if we cancel early, we don't lose the design money. That makes waiting less costly than I thought.

Daniel: Right. But we still lose the season if we wait for the full test. The test takes two weeks. Planting season starts in three weeks. So if we wait, we might still make it—but it's tight.

Maya: So let's summarize. Option A: approve now, no conditions. Option B: postpone until the full test. Option C: approve with conditions—start design, but no construction until the test is acceptable. And we publish what we know.

Priya: I can support Option C. But I want the public note to say clearly that the early scan is not a full test. People might think 'low risk' means 'safe'. That's not the same.

Maya: Agreed. We'll say: 'The early scan suggests low risk, but it is not a full test. The full test will decide.'

Daniel: And one more thing: we should set a date to review the decision. If the test is delayed again, we don't want to wait forever. Let's say we review in four weeks, no matter what.

Maya: Good. So the motion is: approve Option C, with a public note and a review date in four weeks. All in favor?

Priya: Yes.

Daniel: Yes.

Maya: Then it's decided. Thank you both. And remember: we're deciding with incomplete evidence, but we're being honest about it. That's the best we can do today.

grammar.title: 条件句与真实条件：用 if 表达条件和结果

materials.instructions: 项目原创模拟场景与数据，不是官方试卷。阅读文章后独立回答10题，再检查逐题依据。题目包含信息定位、论证范围、比较及推断；遇到词汇可用划词帮助，但使用帮助不算独立测评。语法先看规则，再做新语境练习。
materials.passage:
A. Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about assessing the transferability of research findings. In other words, we ask: can the results of a study conducted in one setting be applied to another setting? This is a crucial question for policymakers, educators, and business leaders who want to use research evidence to make decisions. Let me start with a simple example. Suppose a study finds that a new teaching method improves math scores in urban schools. Can we assume it will work equally well in rural schools? Not necessarily. Transferability depends on many factors, including the characteristics of the population, the context, and the implementation. In this lecture, I will discuss three key criteria for assessing transferability: similarity of context, similarity of population, and fidelity of implementation. I will also explain how to check for stability of results across different studies.

B. First, similarity of context. When we consider whether findings can transfer, we need to compare the original setting with the new setting. Key contextual factors include the physical environment, the organizational culture, and the available resources. For instance, a program that requires high-speed internet may not transfer to a region with poor connectivity. Similarly, a teaching method that relies on small class sizes may not work in schools with large classes. Researchers often use a framework called 'contextual fit' to evaluate how well a program matches a new setting. If the contextual fit is low, transferability is likely to be limited. However, even if the context is similar, we must also consider the population.

C. Second, similarity of population. The people in the new setting may differ from those in the original study in important ways. These differences can include age, prior knowledge, motivation, and cultural background. For example, a study on adult learners may not transfer directly to children, because adults and children learn differently. Likewise, a reading intervention designed for native speakers may not be effective for second-language learners. Researchers therefore recommend that before transferring a program, we should check whether the target population shares key characteristics with the original population. If the populations are very different, the findings may not hold. But even with similar context and population, there is a third criterion: fidelity of implementation.

D. Third, fidelity of implementation. This refers to how closely the program is delivered as intended. Even a well-designed program can fail if it is not implemented correctly. For instance, if teachers do not receive adequate training, they may not use the method as the developers intended. Similarly, if resources are insufficient, the program may be adapted in ways that reduce its effectiveness. High fidelity means that the core components of the program are delivered as planned. Low fidelity can lead to weak or inconsistent results. Therefore, when assessing transferability, we must ask: can the new setting implement the program with high fidelity? If not, the expected outcomes may not be achieved.

E. Now, let me turn to the second part of the lecture: stability of results. Stability refers to whether the findings are consistent across multiple studies. If a single study finds an effect, we should be cautious. But if several studies in different settings find similar effects, we can have more confidence in the results. This is where replication comes in. Replication means repeating a study to see if the results are the same. When results are stable across replications, transferability is more likely. However, we must also be aware of publication bias: studies with positive results are more likely to be published than studies with negative results. This can distort our perception of stability. To check stability, researchers use meta-analysis, which combines the results of many studies. A meta-analysis can reveal whether effects are consistent or whether they vary widely. It can also help identify factors that explain why effects differ, such as variations in context or population. Therefore, stability is not just about whether results are consistent, but also about understanding the conditions under which they hold.

F. Consider a fictional district reviewing an urban pilot. The average test gain was positive, but most participating teachers had volunteered and received weekly coaching. The rural district could offer only monthly support. Treating the average as a promise would conceal two uncertainties: whether the same learners would benefit and whether the essential teaching routines could be sustained. The district proposed a small local trial, recorded which components were delivered, and defined success before examining results. It would report missing responses as well as completed tests. This would not reproduce the original study perfectly, but it would distinguish evidence of local feasibility from an assumption that the published average must recur. Importantly, a null result would also be reported; concealing it would make later reviews of the evidence less informative.

G. In conclusion, assessing transferability requires careful analysis of context, population, and implementation. Stability of results across studies adds further confidence. As you go about your work, I encourage you to ask critical questions: Is the context similar? Is the population similar? Can the program be implemented with fidelity? Are the results stable across studies? By asking these questions, you can make better decisions about whether to apply research findings in new settings. Thank you for your attention. I am happy to take any questions now.

materials.title: Assessing Transferability: A Simulated Lecture on Research Portability
materials.instructions: 本材料为原创模拟练习，不是官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。请先听录音（或阅读转写稿），完成10道听力题；然后学习语法规则并完成8道语法题；最后进行口语和写作迁移练习。听力题中，单选题选出最佳答案；填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制；判断题选择 True、False 或 Not Given，并阅读中文解析理解依据。
materials.transcript:
Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a question that comes up whenever a study works well in one place: can we use it somewhere else? This is the idea of transferability. I'm Dr. Lin, and with me is my colleague Dr. Patel, who will add some comments. Let's start with a simple definition. Transferability means the degree to which the results of a study can be reasonably applied to a different group, setting, or time. It is not the same as copying a method. It is about judging whether the findings still make sense elsewhere.

Dr. Patel: May I add something here? Many people confuse transferability with generalization. Generalization is about how widely results hold for a larger population. Transferability is more practical: it asks whether a specific new context is similar enough for the results to be useful.

Dr. Lin: Exactly. So how do we assess it? I suggest four checks. First, look at the participants. Were they similar to the people in the new setting in age, background, and needs? Second, look at the conditions. Did the original study depend on special resources, such as small classes or extra staff? Third, look at the outcome measures. Did the study measure the same thing that the new setting cares about? Fourth, look at the time. Results from ten years ago may not transfer to today, because the context may have changed.

Dr. Patel: I'd like to give an example. A reading program was tested in three urban schools with class sizes of about eighteen students. It improved reading scores after twelve weeks. A rural school with classes of thirty-five wants to adopt it. The method might still work, but the class size is a different condition. So we cannot assume the same result. We need a small trial first.

Dr. Lin: That's a good point. Notice that Dr. Patel did not say the program would fail. She said we cannot assume the same result. That is an important difference. Transferability is a judgment, not a yes-or-no answer. Sometimes we say 'promising but unproven' in a new context.

Dr. Patel: Another common mistake is to focus only on the average result. A study may report an average improvement of five points, but the improvement may be uneven. Some students gained a lot; others gained nothing. When you transfer the program, you need to ask who benefited most. If the new group looks like the low-gain group, the average may mislead you. This is why we should examine subgroup data when available, not just the overall mean.

Dr. Lin: Right. So a careful assessment asks: who benefited, under what conditions, and why? If we can answer those questions, we can make a reasoned decision. If we cannot, we should be cautious. Now, let me summarize the main message. Transferability is about fit, not about copying. It requires evidence from the new setting, even if that evidence is small. A pilot study is often the best next step. Thank you.
